t: A bone sticking up on top of my shoulder: AC joint dislocation and the hook plate
s: A bump on top of the shoulder after a fall may be an acromioclavicular joint dislocation. Treatment choices by grade, the rationale for hook plate surgery, and its pros and cons.
k: shoulder collarbone clavicle acromioclavicular AC joint dislocation separation hook plate
b: Shoulder A bone sticking up on top of my shoulder: AC joint dislocation and the hook plate Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 31, 2026 Some people come in after falling on the shoulder while cycling or exercising and say, “a bone is sticking up on top of my shoulder.” Often the joint where the outer end of the collarbone meets the acromion of the shoulder blade, the acromioclavicular (AC) joint , has been knocked out of place. How far it is out of place decides the treatment Several ligaments hold the collarbone in this joint. Depending on which ligaments are torn and how badly, we usually use the Rockwood classification, from type 1 to type 6. Grade Condition Usual treatment Types 1–2 Ligaments are stretched or partly torn. Little displacement Brace, ice, pain relievers, rehab. Most improve without surgery. Type 3 The ligaments holding the collarbone are completely torn and the end of the collarbone rides up Non-surgical treatment is often tried first; surgery is considered depending on job, sports and symptoms. Types 4–6 The collarbone rides up a lot or is displaced backward or downward Surgery is recommended in most cases. In short, types 1–2 with little displacement almost never need surgery, type 3 is the range where doctors disagree, and from type 4 up the balance tips toward surgery. Both shoulders before surgery. On the right side of the image (the patient's left), the end of the collarbone sits higher than the acromion. If surgery is done, what are the options? There are two main approaches. Hook plate : a metal plate is laid on top of the collarbone and its hook is passed under the acromion to press the collarbone down. It is easy to align while looking directly at the joint, and because it has been used for a long time its results are well known. Suspension fixation (TightRope, “dog bone,” etc.) : holes are drilled in the collarbone and the coracoid process beneath it, and the two are tied together with a strong cord and button-shaped anchors. In many cases the hardware does not need to be removed later. Fixed with a hook plate. The hook at the left end sits under the acromion and presses the collarbone down. How do the results of the two methods differ? A meta-analysis that pooled studies comparing the two methods in acute type 3–5 dislocations that needed surgery found no meaningful difference in shoulder function scores (Constant, UCLA). Pain scores were slightly lower with suspension fixation. The hook plate also has clear weaknesses. Because the hook sits under the acromion, it can catch or hurt when you raise the arm high. Rarely, the bone of the acromion where the hook rests is worn away. For that reason, once bone and ligaments have healed, usually within a few months, a second operation to remove the plate is needed. Suspension fixation, on the other hand, often needs no hardware removal, but drilling through the coracoid is tricky and loosening of the fixation or re-dislocation has been reported, rarely. So is surgery always better? Not necessarily. In a multicenter randomized study in Canada that split acute type 3–5 dislocations between hook plate surgery and non-surgical treatment, the operated side looked better on X-ray but shoulder function at two years was similar , and in the first few months recovery was actually faster in the non-surgical group. Reoperations were more common on the surgical side. So I do not operate on types 1–2, and for type 3 I decide after talking through job, activity, pain and concerns about appearance. When I do operate, I choose the method that gives that patient the most dependable result; I mostly use the hook plate, whose results are well known and which lets me align the joint precisely while looking at it directly. In return, I always tell patients before surgery that a plate removal operation will be needed. In closing Types 1–2 mostly get better without surgery. Type 3 can go either way, surgical or non-surgical, and we decide together based on your life. If surgery is done , functional results are similar with a hook plate or suspension fixation, and each has pros and cons. Whichever method is used, what matters is that it is one the operating surgeon is familiar with and can do well. This article is general medical information. Treatment can differ depending on the degree of dislocation, associated injuries, age and activity level, so please confirm with an examination. References Pan X, Lv RY, Lv MG, Zhang DG. t: The cause of buttock pain hidden in a lumbar MRI: ankylosing spondylitis
s: A 19-year-old with three years of buttock and pelvic pain, diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis after sacroiliitis was spotted on the coronal view of a lumbar MRI: how inflammatory back pain differs from ordinary back pain, what MRI and HLA-B27 tests mean, and current treatment principles.
k: ankylosing spondylitis sacroiliitis buttock pain pelvic pain back pain HLA-B27 inflammatory back pain
b: Hip & Pelvis The cause of buttock pain hidden in a lumbar MRI: ankylosing spondylitis Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 25, 2025 A 19-year-old man came in with pain in the right buttock and pelvis that had lasted three years. He rated the pain 10 out of 10, and said that on waking his body was so stiff he could not get up right away. Another hospital had treated it as a back problem and taken a lumbar MRI, and he had been told there was nothing seriously wrong with his discs. But the real cause was hiding in that very MRI. The clue in the lumbar MRI Sagittal lumbar MRI. The discs and spinal canal we usually look at show no major problem. Coronal view of the same MRI. Around both sacroiliac joints (arrows) there are signal changes suggesting inflammation. On the sagittal view (from the side) the spine looks nearly normal. But a close look at the coronal view (from the front) shows inflammation in the sacroiliac joints , where the sacrum meets the pelvic bones. A lumbar MRI is usually taken to look at the discs, so the sacroiliac joints at the bottom edge of the image are easy to miss. Confirming it with pelvic X-ray and MRI Pelvic X-ray (arrows: both sacroiliac joints) followed by coronal and axial pelvic MRI. The pelvic X-ray showed whitened, hardened bone around both sacroiliac joints (sclerosis) and small pits in the joint surfaces (erosions), findings that suggest early sacroiliitis. So we took a new pelvic MRI. Coronal pelvic MRI (fat-suppressed). The bone around both sacroiliac joints appears bright. Axial pelvic MRI. Inflammatory signal runs along the sacroiliac joints. This time the bilateral sacroiliitis was even clearer. On examination, the Patrick test, in which the leg is placed in a figure-four position and pressed, caused pain on the right. Strongly suspecting ankylosing spondylitis, we tested for the HLA-B27 gene, and the result was positive . What is ankylosing spondylitis? Ankylosing spondylitis is an immune disease that causes repeated inflammation of the spine and sacroiliac joints. The immune system misfires and attacks the joints and the places where tendons attach to bone. When inflammation recurs for a long time, the vertebrae can fuse with bone and stiffen, called ankylosis , which gives the disease its name. It usually starts between the late teens and the 30s and is more common in men. It is closely linked to the HLA-B27 gene. In a study of 160 Korean patients with ankylosing spondylitis, 96.3% were HLA-B27 positive. On the other hand, about 4–6% of the general population also carry this gene, and most of them never develop the disease. So a positive HLA-B27 alone does not make the diagnosis; symptoms and imaging are considered together. How is it different from ordinary back pain? The pain of ankylosing spondylitis differs from common muscular or disc-related back pain. The Assessment of SpondyloArthritis international Society (ASAS) considers back pain inflammatory back pain when at least four of the five features below are present. Features of inflammatory back pain Common mechanical back pain Starts before age 40 Any age Gradual onset Often starts suddenly after strain Improves with movement Worsens with movement Does not improve with rest Improves with rest Pain at night that eases after getting up and moving Usually less at night Other features can include morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes, buttock pain that alternates between sides, knee or heel pain, and uveitis, a red and painful eye. Why is diagnosis often late? Back and buttock pain is common in young people, and early on X-rays often show no change. In a meta-analysis of 64 studies, it took an average of 6.7 years from the start of symptoms to diagnosis. This patient also went three years without knowing the cause. Even before bone changes appear on X-ray, MRI can show inflammation in the bone around the sacroiliac joints (bone marrow edema). If a young person has back or buttock pain lasting more than three months that matches the features above, it is worth checking the sacroiliac joints too. Treatment and management Ankylosing spondylitis is a condition you live with by controlling the inflammation rather than curing it. It is often treated together with rheumatology, and the main principles of the 2022 international (ASAS-EULAR) recommendations are as follows. Exercise and education: regular stretching and exercise are the foundation of treatment. Swimming, walking and exercises that extend the spine are good, with physical therapy if needed. Quitting smoking: smoking is linked to disease progression, so quitting is important. Anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs): the first-line medicine for pain and stiffness. If they work well and symptoms persist, they may be taken continuously. Biologics: if NSAIDs do not control the disease, injectable drugs such as TNF inhibitors or IL-17 inhibitors are considered. Steroids: long-term systemic steroids are not recommended for spinal symptoms. In closing Back or buttock pain lasting more than three months at a young age, especially pain that is stiff in the morning and eases with movement, can point to ankylosing spondylitis. Even if you have been told your lumbar MRI is normal, the sacroiliac joints may need a separate look. HLA-B27 only helps the diagnosis; a positive result does not mean everyone has the disease. With early diagnosis, and inflammation controlled through exercise and medication, everyday life can be maintained well. This article is general medical information. Diagnosis and treatment can differ with symptoms and test results, so please confirm through a medical consultation. References Sieper J, van der Heijde D, Landewé R, et al. t: Thought to be cellulitis or an ankle sprain, but it was pus inside the bone: Brodie abscess
s: A red, swollen foot or a long-lasting ankle ache may not be a common sprain or cellulitis but a Brodie abscess, a pus pocket inside the bone. Symptoms, imaging, differential diagnosis and treatment, based on two actual cases and a systematic review.
k: bone infection osteomyelitis abscess brodie
b: Fracture & Bone Thought to be cellulitis or an ankle sprain, but it was pus inside the bone: Brodie abscess Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · September 17, 2026 A patient in her 70s came in with a red, swollen top of the foot that first looked like cellulitis. A patient in his 20s with long-lasting ankle pain looked like a common sprain. Both turned out to have Brodie abscess, a pocket of pus inside the bone . In both, a single X-ray changed the diagnosis. What is a Brodie abscess? A Brodie abscess is subacute osteomyelitis in which pus collects locally inside the bone. It was first described in 1832 by the British surgeon Benjamin Brodie and bears his name. The body cannot fully clear the bacteria and walls them off in hard bone, so a rim of whitened, hardened bone forms around the pocket of pus. This disease is easy to miss because it does not look like an acute infection . A systematic review that pooled 407 reported cases up to 2019 found the following. Item Findings of the systematic review Age and sex Many young patients (median age 17), with men about twice as common as women Time to diagnosis A median of 12 weeks after symptoms began Symptoms Pain in 98%, swelling in 53%. 84% had no fever Blood tests Inflammatory markers were raised in fewer than half Causative organism Staphylococcus aureus was the most common at 67% Treatment Surgery in 94% and prolonged antibiotics in 77% Recurrence 15.6% recurred and needed further treatment With no fever and blood tests near normal, it is easy to write it off as a sprain, growing pains or muscle pain, and the diagnosis is delayed. Case 1. A patient in her 70s who looked like cellulitis A 78-year-old woman came in with a red, swollen left foot. My first impression was cellulitis, an infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue. She had previously had plate fixation for fractures of the tibia and fibula above the ankle and a knee replacement on the same side. Ankle X-rays before surgery. In the lower left tibia (right side of the image), the bone around the plate is whitened (a sclerotic lesion). The X-ray showed a sclerotic lesion, whitened bone, on the inner side of the tibia, so I added a CT scan. Coronal CT. The inside of the bone is dissolved. Sagittal CT. The pocket of pus has broken through the membrane covering the bone (the periosteum). The CT confirmed inflammation and a pocket of pus inside the bone, with pus that had broken through the periosteum surrounding the bone and spread outside. That is why the skin was red and swollen. Surgery went as follows. I removed the plate on the outer fibula and, through that space, placed antibiotic cement beads mixed with vancomycin inside the tibia. Antibiotic beads release a high concentration of antibiotic at the site of infection for a long time. AP view after surgery. The fibular plate was removed and antibiotic beads were placed inside the tibia. Lateral view after surgery. The plate on the inner tibia was left in place. I did not remove the plate on the inner tibia. Thinking only of treating the infection, it is best to remove all the metal, but removing this plate as well carried a large risk of the weakened tibia collapsing . International consensus defines infection around a plate as a separate entity, fracture-related infection , and the heart of treatment is balancing control of the infection against keeping the bone strong enough to bear load. After this operation I left myself a note: “in chronic osteomyelitis, watch out for fractures in advance.” Afterward the patient complained of pain in the opposite knee, and a lumbar MRI showed pockets of pus around it too, so she was transferred to a tertiary hospital to continue treatment. In an older patient with a history of other surgery, an infection can spread to other sites, so new pain should not be taken lightly. Additional note A typical Brodie abscess occurs in young people with no surgical history. A patient who is older and has a plate, like this one, is unusual, and the picture overlaps with chronic infection at a previous fracture surgery site. It looks the same in that it forms a pocket of pus with a rim inside the bone. Case 2. A patient in his 20s who looked like an ankle sprain A patient in his 20s came in with ankle pain that had gone on for a long time. He had no clear memory of a fall, yet the pain would not settle. AP view of the tibia. There is a round abnormal shadow just above the ankle. Magnified view. Whitened, hardened bone surrounds the area where bone has dissolved (arrow). The X-ray showed an osteolytic lesion, dissolved bone, in the lower tibia, surrounded by a rim of whitened, sclerotic bone. This is the classic appearance of a Brodie abscess. T2-weighted MRI. The inside of the lesion is bright, suggesting it is filled with fluid (pus). Axial CT. The pocket of pus is dissolving the outer bone (cortex) and leaking out (arrow). On T2-weighted MRI the inside of the lesion was bright, suggesting fluid, that is, pus, and on CT the lesion was seen dissolving the outer cortical bone and leaking out. Taking the findings together, I strongly suspected a Brodie abscess. MRI has one more finding that helps tell it apart: on T1-weighted images, the “penumbra sign,” a thin band slightly brighter than its surroundings along the inner wall of the abscess. In a study of 32 patients with subacute osteomyelitis it was seen in 75%, and it is known as a finding that points toward infection rather than tumor. It can be confused with a tumor On imaging, a Brodie abscess can look like some bone tumors, so telling them apart is essential. Condition Usual site and age What helps tell them apart Brodie abscess Ends of long bones (metaphysis), children and young adults A well-defined pocket of pus with a white rim; the MRI penumbra sign Osteoid osteoma Long bones, ages 10–20 Pain that worsens at night and responds well to anti-inflammatory painkillers, a small central nidus and thick sclerosis Chondroblastoma Very end of long bones (epiphysis), teenagers A well-defined lesion at the bone end near the growth plate Ewing sarcoma Shaft side of long bones, children and adolescents Poorly defined spreading bone destruction, onion-skin periosteal reaction, possibly with fever and weight loss For that reason, treatment includes a biopsy to confirm it is not a tumor. If pus is found in the operating room, a culture is sent, and the lesion is cleaned out by curettage along with aggressive antibiotic treatment. In the systematic review as well, most patients received both surgery and antibiotics and results were generally good, but about 15% recurred and needed more treatment. In closing A Brodie abscess often has no fever and normal blood tests, so persistent localized pain may be almost the only signal. If a young person has pain in the lower tibia or ankle lasting more than a few weeks, it is worth checking with a single X-ray . If a site of previous plate surgery turns red and swollen, it may be a bone infection rather than a simple skin infection. It can look like a bone tumor, so treatment includes a biopsy and a culture. This article is general medical information. The same symptom can have many causes, so if pain or swelling lasts, please have it checked. t: Still in pain after the calcium was drawn out with an injection? Calcific tendinitis and arthroscopic calcium removal
s: Most calcific tendinitis of the shoulder improves with non-surgical care and ultrasound-guided needling. What arthroscopic calcium removal adds when it does not, from studies and a real case.
k: shoulder calcium calcific tendinitis calcification arthroscopy needling
b: Shoulder Still in pain after the calcium was drawn out with an injection? Calcific tendinitis and arthroscopic calcium removal Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 1, 2026 “I woke up from sleep with my shoulder feeling like it was being torn off.” This is what patients with calcific tendinitis often say. Calcium builds up inside the shoulder tendon, and when the body dissolves it, inflammation flares and sudden severe pain follows. Let me say first and clearly: most calcific tendinitis gets better without surgery . This article is not saying that “calcium must always be removed by surgery.” If anything, the opposite. What I want to say is that for a few patients who do not get better after treatment in sequence, arthroscopic surgery has a clear role. Treatment has an order Step Treatment Description Step 1 Medication, injection, exercise Anti-inflammatory painkillers, steroid injection at the inflamed site, and shoulder exercises. Many people get better here. Step 2 Ultrasound-guided calcium aspiration Under ultrasound guidance, a needle is used to break up and wash out the calcium. It is one of the most effective treatments that need no surgery. Extracorporeal shock wave therapy is also an option. Step 3 Arthroscopic calcium removal When the treatments above do not work or complications arise, the calcium is removed under direct arthroscopic vision. Ultrasound-guided aspiration is a well-supported treatment. A systematic review pooling 908 patients found that most improved in pain and function, and in a randomized study comparing it with steroid injection alone, the group that also had aspiration did better at one year. But when the same study was followed to five years, shoulder function in the two groups ended up similar. That means calcific tendinitis tends to get better with time on its own. So there is no reason to rush to surgery from the first treatment. So when is arthroscopic surgery needed? The problem is when treatment in sequence still does not work. Pain continues even after one or two aspirations The calcium is hard or widespread and a needle cannot remove enough of it The calcium has burrowed into the bone beneath the tendon. Aspiration results have been reported to be clearly worse in this case. Other problems are present, such as weakness or a stiff shoulder Infection is suspected after the procedure In such cases, arthroscopic calcium removal has shown good results in several studies. As Korean examples, 30 of 35 patients who had arthroscopic surgery for chronic calcific tendinitis had less pain within six months, and in another Korean study the pain score fell from an average of 6.7 to 1.0 out of 10. Arthroscopy lets us see the condition of the tendon directly, and any tendon defect left after removing the calcium can be repaired on the spot. Being able to wash out the joint thoroughly is another advantage. There are drawbacks too. Surgery and anesthesia are needed, and it usually takes three to six months for the pain to settle completely and function to return. Temporary stiffness after surgery is reported in about 10–20%, so rehab is important. In short, there is as yet no evidence that arthroscopic surgery is a better treatment than aspiration “from the start.” But for patients who do not get better with aspiration, arthroscopic surgery is an evidence-based next step. A real case: pain that continued after two aspirations He is a man in his mid-40s. He was diagnosed with calcific tendinitis of the left shoulder and had calcium aspiration at a local clinic, but the pain continued, and after hearing that infection was suspected he had a second aspiration. The pain still did not settle, and he came to the emergency room with a swollen shoulder and weakness lifting the arm. The shoulder was also stiff and hard to move. MRI before surgery. A signal change is seen at the greater tuberosity, where the supraspinatus attaches. Two aspirations had already failed, and infection was even a possibility. Rather than repeat the same procedure a third time, I judged that it was better to look directly with the arthroscope, remove the calcium and wash out the joint thoroughly. As seen through the arthroscope. The area around the tendon is severely congested, and white calcium shows between the fibers. After removing the calcium. The place where the calcium was has been tidied up. As the pictures show, the tissue around the tendon was red and congested from inflammation, and calcium remained inside the tendon. I could remove it while seeing even the parts a needle can hardly reach. In closing Calcific tendinitis mostly gets better without surgery. Medication, injections and ultrasound-guided aspiration come first. If you have aspiration and still do not get better, if the calcium has burrowed into the bone, or if there are other problems such as infection or weakness, arthroscopic calcium removal is a good next step. Recovery after surgery takes several months, so keeping up with rehab steadily is important. This article is general medical information. Treatment can differ depending on the size and location of the calcium, how long the symptoms have lasted and other conditions, so please confirm with an examination. t: A hip neck broken in her 50s: fixing it with an FNS instead of a joint replacement
s: A 52-year-old's femoral neck fracture from a fall, treated with the FNS (Femoral Neck System): the Garden classification, why young patients keep their own bone instead of getting a joint replacement, a 2,038-patient study comparing the FNS with three screws, the actual operation and aftercare.
k: femoral neck fracture hip fracture FNS femoral neck system cannulated screws Garden avascular necrosis
b: Hip & Pelvis A hip neck broken in her 50s: fixing it with an FNS instead of a joint replacement Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 3, 2026 A 52-year-old woman came in with left hip pain after a fall. Tests showed a femoral neck fracture : a break in the neck just below the head of the thigh bone (femur). In the last column I wrote about a periprosthetic fracture in a patient around 90. Even for the same hip, a patient in her 50s calls for a completely different calculation. This is the story of fixing the fracture to save the patient's own bone instead of replacing the joint, and of choosing a device called the FNS . Why femoral neck fractures are tricky The femoral neck is the short neck that joins the round femoral head to the shaft of the thigh bone. The blood vessels to the head run up along this neck, so when the neck breaks, the blood supply to the head can be cut off. Avascular necrosis: a head that loses its blood supply can slowly collapse. Nonunion: the neck takes large body-weight and twisting forces, so it may fail to heal. In a meta-analysis of 1,558 femoral neck fractures in young patients, avascular necrosis occurred in 14.3%, nonunion in 9.3% and reoperation in 18.0% after surgery. These complications were more common in displaced fractures. That is why accurate reduction and solid fixation matter above all. How far has it shifted? The Garden classification Femoral neck fractures are usually graded by the Garden classification , which asks whether the fracture is complete and how far the head has shifted. Stage I Incomplete fracture Head tilted outward and impacted Stage II Complete fracture Not displaced Stage III Complete fracture Partly displaced; head rotated Stage IV Complete fracture Fully displaced and separated A simplified drawing of the Garden classification. Red lines are fractures; thin lines show the direction of the trabeculae inside the bone. Stages I and II are grouped as undisplaced, stages III and IV as displaced. This patient was about stage III. Preoperative coronal CT. A fracture line runs through the neck just below the left femoral head (right side of the image; arrows). The CT showed a fracture line just below the left femoral head, with the head shifted out of place. It can be read as roughly a Garden stage III fracture. Scrolling through the preoperative CT in several planes. We checked the direction of the fracture line and how far it had shifted, then decided how to fix it. Why a joint replacement is not the first choice in your 50s Displaced femoral neck fractures in older patients are often treated with joint replacement. In the early 50s, though, it is a different story. Replacements wear out, so a young patient is more likely to need at least one revision in their lifetime. For young patients the rule is to reduce the fracture precisely and fix it to save their own femoral head , and not to delay surgery. Two options: three screws or an FNS Feature Three-screw fixation FNS (Femoral Neck System) Component Three large screws placed parallel in an inverted triangle A large bolt + anti-rotation screw + small plate working as one unit Principle Each screw holds the head separately The bolt and plate lock together at a fixed angle (angular stability) Pros Long track record, small incisions, lower cost Designed to resist rotation and bending; allows sliding so the fracture surfaces compress and heal Cons May hold less well when the fracture line is close to vertical A newer device with less long-term data; higher cost What does recent research say? An interesting study appeared in 2025 in the Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (JBJS). Using the hip fracture registry of Kaiser Permanente in the United States, it analyzed 2,038 patients aged 60 and over, comparing the FNS (352 patients) with three-screw fixation (1,686 patients). The rate of reoperation within 2 years was 4.0% for the FNS and 4.8% for screws . The hazard ratio adjusted for several factors was 0.92 (95% confidence interval 0.50–1.71): no statistically significant difference. The result was the same when the comparison was limited to the 72 surgeons who had used both devices. There are caveats. The study included patients aged 60 and over, and this patient was 52. Studies comparing the FNS with screws in young patients alone are mostly small and retrospective. A meta-analysis of them found slightly higher function scores with the FNS and similar neck shortening. My choice: the FNS I used an FNS for this patient. Both methods were evidence-based options, and the difference in reoperation rates in the study was not statistically significant. Still, the number was slightly lower for the FNS (4.0% vs 4.8%). For a young patient whose displaced fracture had to be held firmly in one go, I chose the option that looked even slightly more favorable. The operation After reducing the fracture, we fixed it while checking the position in front and side views on intraoperative fluoroscopy. 1 With the aiming device in place, a guide pin is passed through the center of the femoral neck up to the head. 2 The side view confirms that the pin runs through the middle of the neck. 3 A stepped drill follows the pin to make the path for the bolt. 4 The bolt and small plate are pushed in as one unit. 5 The anti-rotation screw is inserted, and the plate is fixed to the femur with two screws. 6 The final position is checked in the side view. Postoperative X-rays Taken on the way back to the ward after surgery. The bolt and anti-rotation screw reach into the femoral head. A later front view of the pelvis after surgery. The bolt, anti-rotation screw, plate and two screws are visible, and the hip can be compared side by side with the other one. Care after surgery Weight bearing: increased gradually with crutches or a walker, depending on the fracture pattern and fixation. Displaced fractures in young patients often start cautiously. Regular X-rays: avascular necrosis and nonunion can appear 1–2 years after surgery. Even after the bone heals, check-ups continue on schedule in clinic. Symptoms to report right away: if pain in the groin or deep in the buttock returns or worsens, see a doctor without waiting for the next appointment. Bone health: for a woman in her 50s, a fracture from a fall is a good reason to have a bone density test ( osteopenia column ). In closing A femoral neck fracture can cut off blood flow to the femoral head, bringing a risk of avascular necrosis and nonunion. For young patients such as those in their 50s, the rule is to save their own femoral head with precise reduction and solid fixation rather than a joint replacement. In the 2,038-patient study, the FNS and three screws had statistically similar reoperation rates. Accurate reduction and fixation matter more than the device. For 1–2 years after surgery, regular X-rays are taken to check progress. This article is general medical information. Treatment can differ with age, fracture pattern and bone condition, so please confirm through a medical consultation. References Garden RS. Low-angle fixation in fractures of the femoral neck. t: A femur broken in a scooter accident: walking again with an intramedullary nail
s: A teenage femoral shaft fracture treated with an intramedullary nail, with real X-rays of the year it took to heal. Covers fracture classification, why nailing is the standard, rehabilitation by stage, and hardware removal.
k: thigh femur femoral shaft fracture intramedullary nail
b: Fracture & Bone A femur broken in a scooter accident: walking again with an intramedullary nail Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · January 2, 2026 A patient in his late teens came in with severe pain in the left thigh after falling off an electric scooter. The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the body, so a break in its shaft means a very large force was applied. This article follows the course, in real images, from surgery until the bone had fully healed and the metal was removed. Diagnosis: a fracture with a butterfly fragment X-ray before surgery. The shaft of the left femur (right side of the image) is broken and widely displaced. A fracture of the femoral shaft and a detached bone fragment are seen. 3D CT. A butterfly-wing-shaped fragment has broken off between the large upper and lower pieces. The X-ray showed a widely displaced fracture of the femoral shaft, and CT let me examine the shape of the fragments in three dimensions. It was a fracture in which a butterfly-wing-shaped wedge fragment had broken off between the large upper and lower pieces. By the AO/OTA classification widely used for fractures, this is a type B (wedge) fracture . Class Shape Meaning Type A, simple fracture Two bone pieces Subdivided into spiral, oblique and transverse fractures Type B, wedge fracture An additional butterfly-shaped fragment When the wedge fragment is fitted back, the large upper and lower pieces touch each other (this patient) Type C, complex fracture Multiple fragments, or a whole segment Even when fitted together, the large upper and lower pieces do not touch Electric scooters have small wheels, so riders easily fall on small curbs or ice, and a fall at speed produces a high-energy injury close to a motorcycle accident. Fractures with a butterfly fragment or several pieces, as here, are common. Treatment: why an intramedullary nail For femoral shaft fractures in adults and in adolescents who have almost finished growing, surgery is the rule, and the standard treatment is intramedullary nailing , in which a long metal rod is placed in the marrow canal inside the bone. The fracture site is not opened. Because the nail is inserted through small incisions at the hip and knee, the blood clot (hematoma) at the fracture and the surrounding blood supply are preserved, which favors healing. It acts as a pillar inside the bone. The nail shares the body weight with the bone, so walking can begin early. The results have been verified for a long time. In the large 1984 study that established this method, 99.1% of 520 femoral fractures healed and 0.9% became infected. Depending on the entry point, a nail can be inserted through the greater trochanter , the bony prominence on the outer side of the hip, or through the piriformis fossa , the hollow just inside it. In a study comparing the two, healing rates and functional results were similar, but the trochanteric approach had shorter intraoperative fluoroscopy time (average 95 versus 153 seconds) and, in obese patients, shorter operating time. In adolescents with open growth plates, entering through the piriformis fossa risks injuring the blood supply to the femoral head, so I choose the trochanteric entry. For this operation I used a 10 mm diameter, 380 mm long nail inserted through the greater trochanter, and filled the gap between fragments with artificial bone graft. AP view just after surgery. The nail supports the whole femur and is locked with screws above and below. Lateral view just after surgery. The butterfly fragment was not perfectly reduced, but the alignment of the leg was corrected. Why it heals even if the fragment is not perfectly fitted Honestly, looking at the images right after surgery I felt some regret that the butterfly fragment was not an exact anatomical fit. But the heart of femoral shaft fracture surgery is not fitting the fragments 100%, like gluing them. It is correcting length, rotation and alignment , and creating an environment in which the bone can heal on its own. This is called biological fixation . How the bone healed over one year 1 month Callus (new bone) begins to appear around the fracture. 2 months The callus grows denser and bridges the fragments. 4 months The callus hardens and the fracture line fades. 1 year The bone has healed solidly, to the point where the fracture line is almost invisible. In the 1-, 2- and 4-month images, white callus fills in around the fracture, and at one year it had healed so solidly that the fracture line was almost invisible. It is the result of nail fixation that protects the blood supply, combined with a young patient's capacity to recover. Removing the metal after the bone healed AP view after removal. Only the screw holes remain where the nail was. Lateral view after removal. The shape and alignment of the bone are well maintained. I removed the nail after confirming that the bone had healed enough. Whether metal has to be removed, and when, depends on age, site and symptoms. The details are in Do you have to remove the metal plate in your body? . Rehab after surgery: walking again The main goal of nail fixation goes beyond getting the bone to heal: it is to get up and walking as soon as possible . The table below is a general example and is adjusted to the fracture pattern and the rate at which callus forms. Period Goal Main content Just after surgery to 2 weeks Control pain and swelling, prevent joint stiffness Ankle pumps to prevent blood clots, tightening the thigh with the knee straight, starting to bend and straighten the knee 2–6 weeks Walking with crutches Starting at 20–30% of body weight while checking stability on X-ray. In young patients, increase faster if callus fills in quickly 6 weeks to 3 months Off crutches, normal walking If callus is sufficient, full weight bearing, hip and thigh strengthening, stationary bike From 3–6 months Return to sports Start with light jogging, then jumping and cutting sports. Discuss contact sports with your doctor I am often asked, “Do I have to lie in bed until the bone has fully healed?” The answer is no. Appropriate weight bearing stimulates bone cells and in fact helps the bone heal. This patient also rehabilitated actively, and a year later he walks and runs as he did before the accident. In closing A femoral shaft fracture is caused by a large force, and in adults and adolescents intramedullary nailing is the standard treatment. The goal of surgery is less to fit the fragments perfectly than to restore length, rotation and alignment and protect the environment in which the bone heals. The nail lets you walk early, and steady rehab puts the finishing touch on treatment. When riding an electric scooter, always wear protective gear and be careful on ice and curbs. This article is general medical information. Treatment and rehab can differ depending on the fracture pattern, age and associated injuries, so please confirm with an examination. t: Fifth metatarsal base fracture: is a cast always necessary?
s: Treatment options for fifth metatarsal base fractures, often diagnosed after an ankle sprain.
k: foot fifth metatarsal jones fracture cast
b: Foot & Ankle · Fracture & Bone Fifth metatarsal base fracture: is a cast always necessary? Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · December 25, 2025 Sometimes you twist your ankle, go to the hospital, and are given the unfamiliar diagnosis of “fifth metatarsal base fracture.” It is a fairly common injury in which the bony prominence on the outer side of the foot, toward the little toe, is pulled off by a ligament. Once diagnosed, people usually worry about two things: “Do I need surgery?” and “Do I need a cast for a long time?” Surgery is not often needed Acute fractures from a misstep in daily life are mostly treated without surgery. Surgery may be considered, though, when the gap between fragments is wide, when other injuries are present, or in fractures at sites where bone heals poorly, such as an athlete's stress fracture. A cast or a hard-soled shoe Randomized studies comparing a cast with a protective shoe with a firm sole for this fracture have been reported. Pain and bone healing were similar with the two methods, and some results show that return to daily life was somewhat faster with the shoe. The shoe is easier to wash and lighter; the cast gives the reassurance of firm immobilization. What we decide together in clinic Where the fracture is and how far the fragments are displaced Your job, sports and walking plans How much weight to put on the foot during the protection period The protection period is usually given as around a month, but it varies from person to person. Do not stop protection on your own just because the pain lessens; confirm with a follow-up X-ray. This article is general information. Treatment can differ depending on the location and displacement of the fracture, your age and lifestyle, so please confirm with an examination. References Hard-Soled Shoe Versus Short Leg Cast for a Fifth Metatarsal Base Avulsion Fracture: A Multicenter, Noninferiority, Randomized Controlled Trial . J Bone Joint Surg Am . 2021.

t: Hallux valgus: when should you think about surgery?
s: Evaluation of hallux valgus (bunion), shoes and braces, and when to consider surgery, explained from the patient's point of view.
k: big toe bunion hallux valgus
b: Foot & Ankle Hallux valgus: when should you think about surgery? Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 28, 2026 The deformity in which the big toe bends toward the second toe and the bone on the inner side of the foot sticks out is called hallux valgus, or a bunion. Genetic tendency, foot shape and footwear are thought to act together. Not every change in shape needs treatment; pain and difficulty in daily life are the basis for deciding. Assessment in clinic On a standing X-ray I check the angle of the curve and the shape of the bone. Only with weight on the foot can you see the true deformity. I also consider where it hurts, trouble wearing shoes and your usual activity level. What you can try first Switch to shoes with a wide toe box and a low heel Use pads that protect the bump or a spacer between the toes Use anti-inflammatory painkillers when the pain is severe These measures can help reduce pain, but they cannot reverse a bone that has already bent. When surgery is considered We talk about surgery when pain continues even after non-surgical measures have been used well, or when walking in shoes is so difficult that daily life is seriously disrupted. The surgical method differs with the degree of deformity in where and how the bone is cut and realigned, and the surrounding soft tissue is sometimes adjusted as well. The time to put weight on the foot and the recovery period also depend on the method, so it is best to hear the specifics in clinic. What to prepare before the visit One or two pairs of shoes you wear often A note of which movements hurt the most Treatments you have tried so far This article is general information. Treatment can differ depending on the degree of deformity and symptoms, your age and lifestyle, so please confirm with an examination. References American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons. Bunions . t: Do you have to remove the metal plate in your body? When is it removed?
s: Do you really need to remove the plates and screws after fracture surgery? A review of 119 hardware removals among 1,040 operations I performed, explaining when and why.
k: plate screw hardware removal implant removal
b: Fracture & Bone Do you have to remove the metal plate in your body? When is it removed? Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 29, 2026 · Hardware removal seen through 1,040 operations There is a question that people who have had fracture surgery ask most often in the clinic: "Doctor, when does this metal come out? Do I have to remove it?" The answer is "it depends on the person and the site." Saying only that would leave you at a loss, so this time I looked directly at my own surgical records. Of the 1,040 operations I performed at three hospitals from March 2023 to October 2026, the operations the surgical record classified as hardware removal numbered 119 (about 11%) . That is about one in ten, a fairly common operation in orthopedics. Of these, I excluded 16 that were not operations to remove metal from the body, such as removing foreign bodies, calcium or loose bodies in a joint, and looked closely at the remaining 103 below. Where was metal removed most often? Number of hardware removals by site (March 2023–October 2026, 103 operations) The most common sites were the wrist and hand (25) and the ankle and foot (24) . Both are where bones most often break in a fall, and the plate sits right under the skin, so it is easy to feel and to cause discomfort. Next came the clavicle (10) , the kneecap (9) and the plate from high tibial osteotomy, HTO (9) . An HTO plate is not for a fracture; it holds the bone after it has been cut to straighten a bowlegged knee. It is often removed once the bone has healed, because it tends to catch under the skin on the inner side of the knee and would have to come out anyway if a knee replacement is done later. By contrast, there were only 2 removals from the femur . I explain why below. Do you have to remove it? If it causes no trouble, most of the time it does not need to come out. Orthopedic metal used today rarely causes problems even after a long time in the body. Removing metal is a real operation too, so anesthesia, a wound and, rarely, risks such as infection, nerve injury and refracture come with it. But in these cases I recommend removal or actively consider it. When the metal can be felt or hurts : where there is little flesh, such as the outer ankle bone, collarbone, kneecap and tip of the elbow, the metal easily rubs against shoes or bag straps. When infection develops : once bacteria settle on the metal surface, removing the metal is often needed to cure it. When screws loosen or the metal breaks When the metal interferes with joint movement or tendons When another operation is planned : an osteotomy plate is the typical example. When a young, active person wants it : we decide after talking it through thoroughly. On the other hand, there are also cases where it is better not to remove it . A large rod placed for a fracture around the hip is a major operation to take out, and there is a risk of breaking again through the old site, so especially in older patients it is usually left in. That is why there are only two femur removals in my records. In places where a nerve runs right next to the metal, such as the humerus, I also weigh benefits and risks more carefully. When is it removed? There is one principle: after the bone has healed completely and firmly . Only once the bone has rebuilt itself to the point where the fracture line cannot be seen on X-ray can it take over the work the metal was doing. I selected 28 patients whose records include both the fracture surgery and the hardware removal for the same person, and calculated the time between the two operations. Time from fracture surgery to hardware removal (28 patients, median about 6.7 months) The median was about 6.7 months . Half of the patients had the metal removed between about 6 and 11 months . 25 of the 28 patients (89%) fall between 3 and 18 months. By site, there were small differences: the shoulder and upper arm (hook plates, etc.) about 5 months, the clavicle 6 months, the ankle and foot about 7 months, the wrist about 9 months and the elbow about a year. But split by site there are only 3 to 8 patients each, so please treat these as rough tendencies. Also, this calculation can use only records from March 2023 onward, so it does not include people whose fracture surgery was before that or who have not yet had the metal removed. For that reason the true intervals may be longer than shown. Only 1 of the 28 had the metal removed within 3 months. Removal this early happens when discomfort is severe or for a special reason such as reoperation. It does not mean "the sooner the better." What is the removal operation like? It is much lighter than the first operation. Based on my records, it looks like this. (Operating time and hospital stay are from 31 operations in 2026 for which records remain; anesthesia and age are from the 72 with records.) Operating time : median 25 minutes, half between 20 and 40 minutes Anesthesia : mostly regional anesthesia that numbs only the lower body or the arm; general anesthesia in 1 of 72 Hospital stay : median 3 days (counted from admission date to discharge date); some went home after a single day Patient age : median 60 years, with 75% in their 50s to 70s Cautions after removal Right after metal is removed, small holes remain in the bone where each screw was. Until those holes fill back in with bone, that area is relatively weak. For that reason I usually tell people to avoid falls and activities with heavy impact for about 6 weeks to 3 months . How long the holes take to fill depends on the site and age, so talk with your doctor about when to return to sports. Rarely, bone comes away with the metal. I once struggled when bone loss turned out to be greater than expected while removing a screw from a small wrist bone (the scaphoid). That is why the principle "if it does not bother you, do not remove it" matters. Frequently asked questions Can I have an MRI with metal in my body? Most orthopedic metal (titanium, medical stainless steel) is MRI-safe. The image around the metal may be slightly blurred. Be sure to tell the staff before the scan that you have metal in your body. Will it set off airport security? Depending on the size and type of the metal, it may or may not. Even if it does, explaining that it is from surgery usually ends with an extra check. Won't it rust or harm the body if I just leave it? Medical metal is made so that it does not rust in the body. If it causes no trouble, most people can keep it for life with no problem. In closing If it causes no trouble , it mostly does not need to come out. If it is removed, it is after the bone has fully healed , usually between 6 months and a year in my patients. For a few weeks to a few months after removal , do not put stress on the bone. Even the same metal has a different right answer depending on site, age and lifestyle. It is best to decide while looking at the X-ray together with the doctor who operated on you. If you have questions, please write to doctornhs@naver.com . The statistics in this article were compiled, with personal information removed, from 1,040 operations I performed from March 2023 to October 2026. Of the 119 that the surgical record classified as hardware removal, I analyzed 103 after excluding 16, such as removal of foreign bodies, calcium or loose bodies in a joint. The interval calculation is based on the 28 patients for whom both the fixation and the removal were confirmed for the same person. Because these are one doctor's records, please treat them as reference material rather than a general standard. This article is general information, and treatment must be decided through an examination. References Vos DI, Verhofstad MHJ. Indications for implant removal after fracture healing: a review of the literature . Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg . 2013;39(4):327–337. Statistics: 1,040 operations performed by Hee Seung Nam, March 2023 to October 2026 (aggregated with personal information removed).

t: Both shoulders hurt, but the cause was the liver: liver abscess and referred shoulder pain
s: A 66-year-old came in with pain in both shoulders and was diagnosed with a liver abscess by blood tests and CT. The case shows how liver and diaphragm problems can be felt as referred shoulder pain, and the warning signs that call for another cause.
k: shoulder pain referred pain liver abscess diaphragm
b: Shoulder Both shoulders hurt, but the cause was the liver: liver abscess and referred shoulder pain Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · September 16, 2026 A 66-year-old woman came in saying both of her shoulders had hurt for two weeks. When someone in her 60s comes with shoulder pain, I usually think first of frozen shoulder, a rotator cuff tear or calcific tendinitis. But her pain began not in the shoulder but in the liver . The shoulder X-rays were clean X-rays of both shoulders. Nothing is seen in the bones or joints that would explain the pain. On the X-rays of both shoulders I saw nothing in the bones or joints that would explain the pain. On examination she winced when I pressed the trapezius area above the shoulder, but the pattern was a little different from typical shoulder joint disease. When the X-ray is clean and the examination is ambiguous, it is common to move straight on to a shoulder injection or physical therapy. But wondering whether some other cause might be hiding, I ordered blood tests first. The signal in the blood tests Test Result What the test looks at CRP 25.60 The degree of inflammation somewhere in the body. It was greatly raised. ALT 102 An enzyme that leaks into the blood when liver cells are damaged GGT 223 An enzyme that rises when there is a problem in the liver or bile ducts (the channels that carry bile) LDH 280 An enzyme that rises when various tissues, including the liver, are damaged All values in the table are marked as abnormal because they exceeded the normal range of the laboratory that ran the test. Normal ranges differ slightly from lab to lab. CRP, the inflammation marker, was very high, and the liver enzymes were well beyond the normal range. It was a signal that this was not a simple joint problem but an internal medicine problem somewhere in the body that needed to be checked quickly. I immediately requested a gastroenterology consultation, and gastroenterology performed chest and abdominal CT. The cause found on CT: liver abscess Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT. At the tip of the arrow, the broad area at the front of the liver that is darker and mottled compared with its surroundings is the liver abscess. CT is viewed from the patient's feet looking up, so the left of the image is the patient's right. CT confirmed a liver abscess , a pocket of pus inside the liver. The patient was transferred straight to a tertiary hospital and began inpatient treatment. Why does a sore liver cause shoulder pain? The reason is referred pain . Referred pain is the phenomenon of feeling pain in a different part of the body, away from where the real problem is. A well-known example is the pain in the left arm or jaw during a heart attack. The pocket of pus and inflammation at the top of the liver irritate the diaphragm just above. Sensory signals from the diaphragm (especially its central part) travel along the phrenic nerve up to levels 3–5 of the cervical spinal cord (C3–C5). The sensory nerves for the skin over the top of the shoulder and trapezius (mainly C4) enter the spinal cord at the same levels. The brain mistakes the signal for one coming from the familiar shoulder area and feels that the shoulder hurts . Figure. A simplified drawing of how diaphragmatic referred pain works. For that reason, problems around the liver, gallbladder and diaphragm can show up as pain at the tip of the right shoulder or along the ridge between neck and shoulder. The trapezius area that hurt in this patient also overlaps the region served by the C4 nerve. The same thing happens on the left: when the left diaphragm is irritated, for example by a spleen injury, and the left shoulder hurts, it is called Kehr's sign . The liver is on the right, so it usually shows up as right shoulder pain. Why this patient had pain on both sides is hard to say for certain, but we can consider the possibility that the inflammation was widespread or that a systemic inflammatory response was also at work. Such cases are reported steadily. In a Korean case published in the Korean Journal of Pain, a 31-year-old man who improved after a bursa injection for right shoulder pain returned three weeks later with right upper abdominal pain and fever and was diagnosed with a liver abscess. An American emergency medicine journal also published a case in which multiple liver abscesses were found in a 92-year-old who came with pain in the right shoulder, flank and upper abdomen. It means that pain easing briefly after an injection does not necessarily mean the cause has been solved. What kind of disease is a liver abscess? A liver abscess is a disease in which bacteria enter the liver and form a pocket of pus. It can arise through bile duct disease such as gallstones, bacteria can enter from the intestine through the bloodstream, and in many cases no cause is found. It is more likely the older you are and with diabetes or weakened immunity. In Korea, Taiwan and elsewhere in Asia, Klebsiella pneumoniae is the main causative organism. A liver abscess due to this organism can rarely cause an “invasive liver abscess syndrome” that spreads to other organs such as the eye (endophthalmitis), the meninges of the brain or the lungs, so quick diagnosis and treatment are important. The typical symptoms are fever and abdominal pain, but because symptoms and blood test findings are not specific, it is sometimes mistaken for another disease at first. Diagnosis is by ultrasound or CT, which can confirm it in more than 90%. Treatment is usually 2–6 weeks of antibiotics, and when the abscess is large, percutaneous drainage, in which a thin tube is placed through the skin to drain the pus. Abscesses smaller than 3–5 cm are sometimes treated with antibiotics alone. Shoulder pain: when to suspect other causes What I want to stress first is that most shoulder pain is a problem of the shoulder joint and tendons . Internal organs are rarely the cause. But if you have features like those below, we should look at the whole body, not only the shoulder. Feature A problem of the shoulder itself Referred pain from an internal organ Relation to movement Hurts with specific movements; raising or turning the arm is often difficult Pain does not change much when the shoulder moves Accompanying symptoms Usually confined to the shoulder and arm Fever, loss of appetite, upper abdominal pain, shortness of breath, cold sweats and so on Test X-ray, ultrasound and MRI often show the cause Shoulder tests are normal, and the cause shows up on blood tests or chest and abdominal imaging Please be sure to tell me at your visit if: You have a fever, chills or cold sweats You have lost weight for no reason, or have been treated for cancer Shoulder pain gets worse when you breathe deeply or cough Your upper abdomen hurts, it gets worse after a fatty meal, or your eyes or skin have turned yellow The pain continues even when you rest the shoulder, and does not improve with shoulder treatment If you have tightness in the chest with pain spreading to the left shoulder, arm or jaw and cold sweats, it may be a heart problem. In that case do not wait for an appointment; call 119 (emergency services) right away. Items such as fever, weight loss and a history of cancer are also listed as warning signs that call for further tests in the British Medical Journal (BMJ) primary care guidance on shoulder pain. In closing If the shoulder X-ray is normal but the pattern of pain is not typical, causes outside the shoulder should also be considered. Problems of the liver, gallbladder and diaphragm can be felt as pain at the top of the shoulder through the phrenic nerve (C3–C5) . In this patient a simple blood test showed abnormal inflammation and liver markers, which led to a quick CT diagnosis of liver abscess and then to treatment. If fever, weight loss, pain that worsens with breathing, or upper abdominal pain come with it, please be sure to mention it at your visit. I am a doctor who looks at shoulders, but I try not to look only at the shoulder. I wish the patient a speedy recovery. This article is general medical information based on a single case. Most shoulder pain is a problem of the shoulder itself, and the exact cause should be confirmed through an examination. References Mitchell C, Adebajo A, Hay E, Carr A. t: A 'pop' in the knee on a downhill walk: a radial meniscus tear and arthroscopic repair
s: MRI, arthroscopic repair and postoperative rehabilitation of a radial meniscus tear diagnosed after a knee twist while walking downhill.
k: knee meniscus cartilage tear arthroscopy root repair
b: Knee A 'pop' in the knee on a downhill walk: a radial meniscus tear and arthroscopic repair Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 28, 2026 Many people hurt a knee unexpectedly while walking or hiking and come to the hospital. Today I introduce a case of a 'radial tear of the meniscus' for which surgery is actively considered. Patient case and diagnosis He is a 54-year-old man. He twisted his knee going downhill, felt a 'pop' with severe pain, and came in. The pain continued afterward and he could not walk normally. The McMurray test, which checks for a meniscus injury, was clearly positive and the pain was severe, so I took an MRI right away to confirm the exact cause. MRI findings Knee MRI; the arrow marks the meniscus tear Another MRI slice of the same patient MRI confirmed a radial tear of the meniscus. The meniscus of the knee spreads body weight and absorbs shock. Its fibers are arranged in a circular direction and resist the pressure on the knee (hoop tension); a radial tear splits across these fibers. It is like a rubber band that has snapped, and if left alone the meniscus can lose its shock-absorbing function. It is known to have a worse outlook than other tear patterns and can bring on degenerative arthritis early even at a young age, so where possible I consider restoring it by repair. The arthroscopic procedure Before repair, the arthroscopic view showing the radial tear After repair, sutured with a double-arm needle Looking inside the knee with the arthroscope, the radial tear, in which the meniscus was split from the inside toward the outside, was clear, just as on MRI. A split meniscus must be fixed firmly back in place to regain its original function. After bringing the opened edges together precisely, I sutured them with a double-arm needle. I focused on restoring the anatomy so that the torn meniscal fibers could regain their original tension. Rehab after surgery In a radial tear the repaired site is under a lot of force from body weight trying to pull it open again. That is why care in the first 4 to 6 weeks is especially important. What follows is a general example and can vary with the tear pattern and surgical method. Up to 4 weeks after surgery (protection and healing) : wear a knee brace and walk on crutches without putting the foot down. The angle of knee bending is also usually limited to within 90 degrees so as not to stress the repair. 4 to 6 weeks (partial weight bearing) : with the brace on, begin practicing putting weight on the foot gradually, starting from the toes, and increase the bending angle little by little. After 6 weeks (full weight bearing and strengthening) : remove the brace and crutches and practice normal walking. Build up the thigh muscle weakened after surgery (the quadriceps) with a stationary bike and light strengthening. Serious exercise such as jogging or hiking is tried in stages, usually after 3 to 6 months depending on recovery. In closing A damaged meniscus often has trouble healing on its own. A radial tear in particular can lead to rapid progression of arthritis if left, so treatment that saves the original meniscus wherever possible is important. If the pain does not settle after a 'pop' in the knee, I recommend seeing an orthopedist without delay. If you have questions, please write to doctornhs@naver.com . This article is general information. Surgical results and recovery time differ from person to person with the tear pattern, age and activity level, and the treatment method must be decided through an examination.
