t: A meniscus root tear seen through the arthroscope, and how it is tied back
s: What a meniscus root tear really looks like inside the knee, explained with arthroscopic photos before and after transtibial pull-out root repair.
k: knee meniscus cartilage tear arthroscopy root repair
b: Knee A meniscus root tear seen through the arthroscope, and how it is tied back Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 30, 2026 In the previous article ( If you heard a 'pop' on the stairs: meniscus root tear ) I compared the 'root' of the meniscus to the iron hoop on a wooden barrel. Today I want to show arthroscopic pictures of a knee in which that hoop has broken. The images are part of the records of a patient I operated on, chosen so that no one can be identified. The 'torn root' seen inside the knee Image 1 Before repair. The back end of the medial meniscus has come away from where it should be attached to the bone, leaving a gap. The rounded surface at the top of the arthroscopic screen is the end of the thighbone, and the bottom is the meniscus resting on the shinbone. Normally the back end of the meniscus should be firmly attached to the center of the shinbone, but in this knee that spot is empty and the end of the meniscus hangs ragged. It can be diagnosed on MRI too, but seeing it with the arthroscope makes it immediately clear why people say the 'root has been pulled out.' In this state, when weight is applied the meniscus is pushed outward and cannot act as a cushion. How is it tied back? This patient did not have severe arthritis, so I performed a root repair to reattach the root to its original place. In brief, the method is as follows. Clean up the damaged tissue at the end of the detached meniscus and at the bone site where it was originally attached. Pass strong sutures through the end of the meniscus several times. Drill a small tunnel from the front of the shinbone to the site of the original root. Pull the sutures down through the tunnel to draw the end of the meniscus back into place, then tie them over a small metal button on the front of the shinbone to fix them. Image 2 The sutures passed through. The blue sutures are threaded through the end of the meniscus, and they will be pulled into the bone tunnel. After the repair is complete Image 3 After repair. The end of the meniscus has been pulled back to its original root site and reattached to the bone. When the sutures are pulled and fixed, the end of the meniscus is drawn into the empty spot and attached. It is as if the broken end of the hoop had been driven back into the barrel. Only then can the meniscus regain its ability to hold up when weight is applied (hoop tension). But attaching it in the operating room is not the end. It takes time for the pulled-down root to actually settle into the bone. That is why for about a month after surgery I tell patients to use crutches without putting weight on the leg, and to avoid deep knee bending for several months. Half of the result of surgery depends on how well this period is respected. Why I show the photographs We often hear that “the meniscus is torn,” but it is hard to imagine what that looks like inside the knee. If you see the torn site and the repaired site directly, I think it will be a little easier to feel why you should not dismiss it as “a bit better,” and why the crutch period after surgery has to be kept. Not every root tear can be repaired this way. If arthritis is far advanced or the legs are strongly bowed, I consider other treatments. The treatment choices are laid out in If you heard a 'pop' on the stairs: meniscus root tear . This article is general medical information, and the surgical method and rehab schedule can vary with the condition of the knee and the hospital. If you have symptoms, please consult an orthopedic specialist. It contains surgical photographs. References Lee DW, Ha JK, Kim JG. Medial Meniscus Posterior Root Tear: A Comprehensive Review . Knee Surg Relat Res . 2014;26(3):125–134. Moon HS, Choi CH, Jung M, et al. Medial Meniscus Posterior Root Tear: How Far Have We Come and What Remains? Medicina . 2023;59(7):1181.

t: If you heard a 'pop' on the stairs: meniscus root tear
s: A 'pop' behind the knee when squatting or going down stairs. A meniscus root tear is easy to dismiss because the pain eases after a few days.
k: knee meniscus cartilage tear arthroscopy root repair
b: Knee If you heard a 'pop' on the stairs: meniscus root tear Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 30, 2026 There is something I hear often in clinic. “I squatted down while working in the field and felt a 'pop' behind my knee. It hurt terribly for a few days, but now it is a little better.” I hear this especially from women in their 50s and 60s. And it is the “a little better” that worries me most. When an MRI is taken, a good many of them have a meniscus root tear . What is the 'root' of the meniscus? Inside the knee, between the thighbone and the shinbone, there are two crescent-shaped menisci, one on the inner side and one on the outer side. They are cushions that absorb shock and spread the load when weight is applied. Both ends of this crescent are firmly tied to the shinbone, and this part is called the root . Think of the iron hoop around a wooden barrel. Just as the ends of the hoop must be fastened for the barrel not to spread apart, the meniscus holds up under weight without being pushed outward only if its roots are attached. Normal: the roots at both ends are firmly tied down Posterior root tear of the medial meniscus: the hoop has come undone and is pushed outward from its original position (dotted line) Diagram of the knee seen from above (top of the shinbone). The red dots are where the meniscus roots attach to the bone. Why does it tear with a 'pop'? In young people, meniscus tears often come from a large force during sports. A tear of the posterior root of the medial meniscus, by contrast, often happens after middle age, in a meniscus already weakened bit by bit, during a very minor movement . When getting up from a squat When going down stairs or a downhill slope When sitting cross-legged, or just walking The 'pop' sound or feeling that patients remember is this very moment. Afterward the back or inner side of the knee hurts, especially going down stairs. Why “it's better, so it must be fine” is dangerous The severe pain of the first few weeks usually settles. That is why many people let it pass. The problem is that changes continue inside the knee in the meantime. A meniscus with a torn root is like a barrel whose hoop has come off. The shape remains, but it cannot bear the load and is pushed out of the joint. Biomechanical studies regard a completely torn root as a state similar to removing the whole meniscus . When bone and cartilage strike each other directly where the cushion has gone, the following can happen. Degenerative arthritis progresses faster than expected Tiny stress fractures form just under the bone surface and the pain suddenly becomes severe The time at which an osteotomy or knee replacement is needed comes sooner How is it diagnosed? The meniscus is not visible on a plain X-ray. The X-ray is used to check the joint space, the alignment of the leg and the degree of arthritis, and the root tear itself is diagnosed with MRI . On MRI you can see that the place where the root should be looks empty, or that the meniscus has been pushed out of the joint. If back-of-the-knee pain continued after a 'pop,' I recommend being examined at least once even if the pain has eased. The time when there are the most treatment choices is right after the injury. How is it treated? Not every root tear is operated on. Treatment differs by age, how far the arthritis has advanced and whether the leg is bowed. Condition of the knee Treatment mainly considered Little arthritis, with fairly straight leg alignment Meniscus root repair : the torn root is tied with sutures and pulled through a small tunnel in the bone to be fixed again Arthritis is not severe, but the bowlegged alignment is clear Osteotomy plus root repair : shifts the weight concentrated on the inner side outward to protect the repaired root Arthritis is already far advanced Conservative treatment such as pain control and exercise therapy, and if needed joint replacement (partial or total) Older patients, or when surgery is difficult Medication, injections, strengthening exercises, weight management, temporary use of crutches In the past, partial meniscectomy, cutting out the torn part, was often done, but studies showing that it does not stop progression of arthritis in root tears have appeared and it is rarely recommended now. For a knee in which the root can be fixed, the principle is to reattach rather than cut out . What about after surgery? A root repair needs time for the reattached site to heal. It differs by hospital and surgical method, but usually for a little over a month after surgery you use crutches and do not put weight on the leg. Deep knee-bending movements are also restricted for a period. I tell patients to avoid squatting and sitting cross-legged for several months or more. Repair does not stop arthritis completely. But there are many reports that by helping the meniscus act as a cushion again it slows arthritis and helps delay knee replacement. What you can do for your knees starting today Cut down on squatting and sitting cross-legged : deeply bent positions put the most strain on the back root of the meniscus. Use a low stool for fieldwork or hand-washing laundry. Take the elevator rather than the stairs : the load is especially great going down. Thigh strengthening exercises : if the muscle at the front of the thigh is strong, the shock reaching the knee is reduced. Weight management : studies suggest that losing 1 kg lowers the load on the knee by about 4 kg when walking. In closing Going through my surgical photo folders, I found far more meniscus root tear cases than I expected. A good many of them were patients who said, “it hurt at first, but it got better so I just carried on.” If you heard a 'pop' behind your knee and going down stairs has been uncomfortable since, have it checked once even if the pain has eased. Even for the same knee, the treatment differs depending on when it is found. This article is general medical information, and diagnosis and treatment can differ with the individual's condition. If you have symptoms, please consult an orthopedic specialist. References Lee DW, Ha JK, Kim JG. Medial Meniscus Posterior Root Tear: A Comprehensive Review . Knee Surg Relat Res . 2014;26(3):125–134. Moon HS, Choi CH, Jung M, et al. Medial Meniscus Posterior Root Tear: How Far Have We Come and What Remains? Medicina . 2023;59(7):1181.

t: The first signal your bones send: osteopenia
s: What to check and how to manage osteopenia found on a health checkup, summarizing the author's op-ed for Bridge Economy.
k: osteoporosis osteopenia bone density weak bones
b: Fracture & Bone The first signal your bones send: osteopenia Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 29, 2026 October 20 is World Osteoporosis Day. Osteoporosis has no obvious symptoms in its early stage, so many people learn they have it only after a fracture. That is why a finding of 'osteopenia' on a health checkup is a first warning sign that should not be ignored. What is osteopenia? Osteopenia is the stage before osteoporosis, a state in which bone density is lower than normal but has not yet reached the criteria for osteoporosis. It is classified by the T-score of a bone density test as follows. T-score Diagnosis -1.0 or above Normal Below -1.0 and above -2.5 Osteopenia -2.5 or below Osteoporosis Not all osteopenia progresses to osteoporosis. But bone density outside the normal range means the bones have begun to weaken. Even with the same osteopenia, fracture risk differs greatly with age and the risk factors below. A history of fracture A family history of hip fracture in a parent Long-term steroid use Coexisting conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis Smoking and drinking What to check after the diagnosis Look back at past fractures. If you have ever broken a wrist, spine or hip just from falling from standing height (a fragility fracture), it should not be written off as a simple accident. Even if bone density is in the osteopenia range, a confirmed fragility fracture of the spine or hip allows a diagnosis of osteoporosis and treatment, and medication is also considered when fracture risk is high. Look at the trend in bone density. A single T-score shows only the present state. The amount of decline compared with earlier tests, menopausal status, medications and coexisting conditions should be reviewed together. Results differ with the equipment and the site measured, so rather than fretting over changes in the decimal point, it is better to set the timing of follow-up tests according to your individual risk. Prevention in daily life Diet : rather than relying on a single calcium supplement, eat a balanced diet that includes calcium, vitamin D and good-quality protein. Exercise : steadily combine weight-bearing exercise such as walking with strength and balance exercise. Preventing falls : in older people, not falling is as important as strengthening the bones. Clear away slippery floors, thresholds and dim lighting, and be especially careful in wet bathrooms. In closing Osteopenia is not a result that says 'it's not osteoporosis yet, so it's fine'; it is closer to a preliminary warning that you must manage the risk of osteoporosis and fractures going forward. Rather than treating after a fracture, checking risk factors and protecting the bones from the osteopenia stage is the starting point of lifelong bone health. This article summarizes a piece I contributed to Bridge Economy [Expert Column], “The first signal your bones send, 'osteopenia'… do strength exercise and check bone density” (October 13, 2026; in Korean): link . This article is general information. Interpreting bone density results and whether to treat depend on age, fracture history and coexisting conditions, so please confirm through an examination. References Nam HS. [Expert Column] The first signal your bones send, 'osteopenia'… do strength exercise and check bone density (in Korean). Bridge Economy. October 13, 2026.

t: If the leg with a hip replacement breaks: periprosthetic fracture and revision surgery
s: A periprosthetic fracture of the femur around a hip replacement, explained through the real case of a 90-year-old patient: the Vancouver classification, why revision is chosen for a B2 fracture with a loose stem, surgery with a long modular stem and a grip plate, and aftercare and prevention.
k: periprosthetic fracture hip replacement hemiarthroplasty bipolar revision Vancouver B2 modular stem thigh bone femur
b: Hip & Pelvis If the leg with a hip replacement breaks: periprosthetic fracture and revision surgery Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 3, 2026 Hip replacement is a good operation that relieves pain and gets people walking again. But years later, after a fall or as the bone weakens, the thigh bone that holds the implant can break. This is called a periprosthetic fracture . This is the story of a patient around 90 years old who had previously had a right hip hemiarthroplasty (bipolar). The thigh bone around the implant stem broke, and we performed a revision: the old stem was removed and replaced with a longer one. In this operation I used a modular revision stem for the first time, and I describe that experience here too. What is a periprosthetic fracture? As the name says, it is a fracture of the bone around (peri-) an implant (prosthesis). With hip replacements it usually occurs in the thigh bone (femur) that holds the metal stem. Falls: the most common cause. In older people with osteoporosis, even a minor fall can cause a break. Where stress concentrates: force gathers where the stiff metal stem meets softer bone, especially at the tip of the stem. Weakened bone: over time the bone around the stem can thin or the stem can loosen, leaving the bone vulnerable to small impacts. This is not a minor fracture. In a study of 328 periprosthetic femur fractures across 16 Scottish hospitals in 2019, the average patient age was 79 and one-year mortality was 20.8%. That is lower than for ordinary hip fractures (29%), but 2.7 times higher than in the general population of the same age. That is why early diagnosis and treatment that gets patients up again quickly matter. How treatment is decided: the Vancouver classification Periprosthetic fractures are grouped by the Vancouver classification . The key questions are where the fracture is and whether the implant stem is still firmly fixed . Type A Greater or lesser trochanter Stem left in place; small fixation if needed Type B1 Around the stem; stem well fixed Fracture fixed with plate and cables Type B2 Around the stem; stem loose Revision with a long stem ± fracture fixation Type B3 Loose stem + poor bone stock Revision with bone augmentation; major reconstruction Type C Well below the stem tip Stem left in place; fracture fixed alone A simplified drawing of the Vancouver classification. Red lines are fractures; the orange dotted line means the stem has loosened. This patient had a type B2 fracture. Type B, around the stem, is the most common and the hardest to judge. If the stem is firm (B1), only the broken bone is fixed with a plate and cables. If the stem is loose (B2), fixing the bone alone leaves the stem wobbling, so the rule is revision: remove the stem and replace it with a longer one that passes the fracture and reaches healthy bone . If too little bone remains (B3), a larger reconstruction is needed. This patient: a B2 fracture with a loose stem Preoperative front view. The bone on the outer side of the stem has split off in a long piece, and the fracture line runs down near the stem tip. Preoperative side view. With the bone around the stem broken, nothing is left to hold the stem. The X-ray showed the upper femur around the stem split lengthwise. With the bone that held the stem broken, the stem could no longer be considered stable. This is a Vancouver type B2 fracture. Preoperative CT. 3D images and several slices (yellow arrows) showed how far down the fracture ran and how many fragments there were, and we planned the operation from them. It is hard to tell from X-rays alone how far down the fracture runs, so we took a CT. The new stem must anchor in solid, unbroken bone well below the fracture, so this information is where surgical planning starts. Surgery: remove the stem, bind the bone, insert a longer stem Removing the old stem: the loose hemiarthroplasty stem was taken out. Reducing the broken bone: the greater trochanter (the bony bump on the outside of the hip) and the long split fragment on the outer side were put back in place, then bound with a grip plate that hooks over the trochanter, and cables. The hip muscles attach to the greater trochanter, so it has to heal well for the patient to walk without a limp. Inserting a long stem: a long revision stem was inserted past the fracture to anchor in the solid bone below. Bone graft and the joint: gaps in the bone were filled with graft, and because the cartilage on the pelvic side was in good shape, a hemiarthroplasty (bipolar) head was fitted again. Postoperative front view. The long stem passes the fracture into the bone below, and the greater trochanter and outer fragment are fixed with the grip plate and cables. Postoperative side view. The stem tip sits well below the fracture line, and the cables hold the split bone around the stem. Component What was used Role Revision stem Modular conical stem, distal length 155 mm, diameter 17 mm Anchors in solid bone below the fracture and carries body weight Proximal body 23 mm, length +10 mm Sets leg length and joint position separately Head 28 mm ceramic head + 50 mm bipolar Hemiarthroplasty, leaving the pelvic side as it is Plate Greater trochanteric grip plate (6 holes) Fixes the greater trochanter and outer fragment Cables 7 (3 attached to the plate, 4 free) Bind the split bone around the stem Bone graft 15 cc cancellous allograft Fills gaps to help the bone heal A modular stem, used for the first time What made this operation unusual was the use of Stryker's Restoration Modular system. It was my first time using it. An ordinary stem is a single piece. A modular stem is assembled from a separately chosen distal stem and proximal body . First, a long, fluted, conical distal stem is driven firmly into the unbroken femur to achieve fixation. Then a proximal body of the right length and orientation is chosen to set leg length and joint position. In a periprosthetic fracture the upper bone is broken, so the usual bony landmarks for judging height are gone. Being able to get fixation from below and set leg length from above, separately, suits this situation well. Because the system was new to me, I measured stem length and diameter on X-rays several times before surgery, and during surgery I checked length and stability with trial components before inserting the final implants. There is evidence behind it. In a Mayo Clinic study of 44 patients with B2 and B3 fractures treated with this kind of modular conical stem and followed for an average of 4.5 years, 98% of fractures healed and 98% of stems were stably fixed. However, 11% needed reoperation for dislocation, a reminder that dislocation must be watched for after surgery. Does a B2 fracture always require changing the stem? Not always. Depending on the stem type and fracture pattern, there are reports that precise fixation of the bone alone can be enough. But the evidence from studies comparing the two is still weak. In this patient, the bone that held the stem was itself shattered, so we judged it unwise to leave the stem in place. Care after surgery For older patients the most important goal is getting out of bed as early as possible . Long bed rest quickly brings pneumonia, blood clots, pressure sores and loss of strength. Weight bearing: increased gradually with a walker, depending on the fixation and bone quality, and advanced as X-rays show the bone healing. Preventing dislocation: avoid bending the hip deeply or crossing the leg inward. Details are in the discharge guide after hip replacement . Osteoporosis treatment: keep up bone density testing and medication to prevent the next fracture ( osteopenia column ). Prevention is the best treatment Fall prevention: non-slip mats, bathroom grab bars and a night light, plus a cane or walker if needed. Osteoporosis care: check bone density regularly and keep up calcium, vitamin D and medication. Strength exercise: regular training of the hip and thigh muscles improves balance and lowers the risk of falls. Regular checkups: even after a hip replacement, have regular X-rays to make sure the stem has not loosened. When to come in right away: if, after a fall, the thigh of the replaced hip hurts or you cannot put weight on the leg, see a doctor right away. In closing Periprosthetic fractures mostly result from falls, and in older patients they can be life-threatening. Treatment depends on where the fracture is and whether the stem is firm . For a B2 fracture with a loose stem, revision to a long stem is the rule. A modular stem lets the surgeon get fixation from below and set leg length from above separately, which helps when the bone is broken. Fall prevention and osteoporosis treatment are the surest ways to prevent it. This article is general medical information. Treatment can differ depending on the fracture pattern, bone condition and overall health, so please confirm through a medical consultation. References Duncan CP, Masri BA. t: A lump you can feel: lipoma or sarcoma?
s: Most lumps you can feel are benign, such as lipomas, but rarely one is a sarcoma. Warning signs by size, depth, growth rate and pain, the order of ultrasound, MRI and biopsy, and why a lump should not be cut out casually.
k: lump tumor lipoma sarcoma biopsy
b: Tumor A lump you can feel: lipoma or sarcoma? Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 31, 2026 “I felt a lump in my thigh in the shower. Could it be cancer?” It is a question I hear often in clinic. Let me start with the reassuring part. Lumps you can feel are mostly benign . Only very rarely a malignant tumor called a sarcoma is mixed in, and at first a sarcoma looks almost the same as a lipoma from the outside. What troubled me most while caring for bone and soft tissue tumor patients during residency was that the size of the later operation can change greatly depending on the order in which a lump was first investigated and treated. This article lays out how to tell lumps you need not worry about from lumps you must check. 99 of 100 lumps are benign According to a review in the BMJ, soft tissue tumors of the limbs are about 100 times more often benign than malignant . The most common is the lipoma, a lump of fat, followed by the ganglion cyst around joints, the epidermoid cyst under the skin and the schwannoma arising from nerves. Figure 1. The ratio of benign to malignant soft tissue lumps shown as dots. Benign lumps, including lipomas, are overwhelmingly common. A sarcoma is a malignant tumor that arises in connective tissue other than bone, such as muscle, fat, nerve, blood vessel and fibrous tissue. It is rare, about 1% of all adult cancers, and there are dozens of subtypes. The problem is that most are painless . Because it does not hurt, people assume “it must be a lipoma,” and often come to the hospital only after it has grown large. How deep it lies matters Under the skin there is a layer of fat, and beneath it the tough membrane that wraps the muscle, the fascia . Whether a lump is above or below the fascia is the first fork in the road. Figure 2. The layers under the skin. ① A shallow lump in the subcutaneous fat above the fascia is mostly benign, such as a lipoma. ② A deep lump within or between muscles below the fascia calls for a detailed work-up regardless of size. The ultrasound guidance of the British Sarcoma Group (BSG) explains that a fatty lump in the layer of fat just under the skin is rarely malignant even if it looks slightly unusual on ultrasound. Conversely, a lump deep below the fascia, or a lump that grew back after being removed, is more likely to be a sarcoma. Lumps to worry about: four signs The warning signs that UK and European sarcoma guidelines have in common are as follows. If even one applies, it is best to check with imaging. 5 cm or larger Be careful if it is bigger than a golf ball (about 4.3 cm). A typical lipoma in the subcutaneous fat may be an exception. Deep, below the fascia A lump within or between muscles needs to be checked regardless of size. Gradually getting bigger If you can feel it growing over weeks or months, it is the most important sign. Painful, or came back after removal A lump that has become painful, or that came back in the same spot after surgery, also needs to be checked. The UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends that adults with a growing lump of unknown cause have an ultrasound within two weeks. The European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) guideline also recommends that a superficial lump larger than 5 cm, or a deep lump, be checked with imaging and biopsy. There are liposarcomas that look like lipomas Not every lump made of fat is a lipoma. Among fatty tumors that grow large in deep places, such as between thigh muscles, some are atypical lipomatous tumors (well-differentiated liposarcoma). They almost never spread elsewhere, but if removed incompletely they grow back and, rarely, can change into a more aggressive form. In a study by a German team that compared 113 fatty tumors with MRI and genetic testing, there was not a single atypical lipomatous tumor in the fat layer under the skin, and most lay between muscles. On MRI, septa thicker than 2 mm , areas that brighten with contrast and very large size were the suspicious findings, and the final confirmation is made by finding MDM2 gene amplification in tissue. Common lipoma Atypical lipomatous tumor, liposarcoma Location Often in the fat layer under the skin Between muscles, deep below the fascia Size Usually under 5 cm May grow to 10 cm or more MRI Uniform fat, thin septa Thick septa, nodules, contrast enhancement Treatment Simple removal if bothersome A planned operation, with follow-up needed There is an order to the tests Figure 3. The order of tests when a lump is found. If there are warning signs, MRI and biopsy come before surgery. Ultrasound : the first test. It shows the depth and size of the lump, its internal appearance and blood flow. A typical shallow lipoma or ganglion cyst can mostly be judged on ultrasound alone. MRI : if there are warning signs or the ultrasound finding is unclear, MRI is used to check the extent and nature of the tumor and its relation to nearby nerves and vessels. Biopsy : a bit of tissue is taken with a thick needle to confirm the diagnosis. Because the biopsy tract must also be removed with the tumor later, the principle is that the team that will do the final surgery plans where the needle goes in . In a study by the Musculoskeletal Tumor Society in the United States that analyzed 597 patients, when the biopsy was done somewhere other than a tumor treatment center, diagnostic errors and complications were 2 to 12 times more frequent. In 19% of all patients, treatment became more complicated because of biopsy problems, and there were 18 amputations that could have been avoided. Why “let's just take it out first” is dangerous Sometimes a small, soft lump is removed without imaging and the biopsy then shows a sarcoma. In a meta-analysis (2024) of such unplanned excisions, when a wide re-excision was done, about 60% still had tumor remaining , and the five-year local recurrence risk was higher than with planned surgery. To be fair, in this study there was no meaningful difference in overall survival. But to get rid of the remaining tumor you have to operate again much more widely than the first time, and radiation treatment is added in some cases. If sarcoma had been kept in mind and planned for from the start, it could have been done in one operation. That is why the principle is to get imaging first, before removing a lump that has warning signs . In closing Lumps you need not worry too much about : a lump just under the skin that is small and soft, has stayed the same size for years and does not hurt is mostly a lipoma. Even so, have it checked once with an examination and ultrasound. Lumps you must check : 5 cm or larger, deep below the fascia, getting bigger, painful or recurrent. If even one of these applies, check with ultrasound and MRI, and if needed have a biopsy by a team experienced in tumor treatment. The order matters : imaging, then biopsy, then surgery. Following this order alone can change the outcome of sarcoma treatment. This article is general medical information. The tests and treatment needed can differ with the location and size of the lump and the imaging findings, so please confirm through an examination. References Mannan K, Briggs TW. s: A one-line memo added after a folder name when surgery is over. An orthopedic surgeon takes out a few of his own "I should have..." notes.

b: Notes A surgeon's “I should have...” notes Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 29, 2026 My computer has several hundred surgical photo folders. When an operation is finished I name the folder, and I have a habit of adding one line after the date and the name of the operation. “Should have...” “Look at...” “Next time, like this.” It is not written to show to anyone. It is a note to myself, left so I can open it again the night before the next operation. Today I want to take out a few of those notes. I have changed the details so that the patients cannot be identified. My PC › Surgical photos › 2023–2026 Case Notes Patellar fracture internal fixation — Be careful if it feels too tight. Be sure to look at the skyline view Medial meniscus posterior horn root tear — Should have just drilled the bone tunnel Periprosthetic femur fracture — Should have used a slightly smaller screw Arthroscopic rotator cuff repair — I think I did it well, in my own opinion There is always one line after the name of a surgical photo folder. Part of the actual folders, redrawn so that patients cannot be identified. 01 “Be careful if it feels too tight. Be sure to look at the skyline view” It was a patient with a broken kneecap (patella). The operation is to fit the broken fragments together and fix them with cannulated screws. The cannula placed along the path of the screw felt like it was biting tightly into the bone, and I took that feeling as a sign that it was “gripping well.” But on the post-operative images, the upper screw was touching the cartilage surface on the inner side of the kneecap. It was at an angle that could not be seen on the front and side images alone. If I had taken the skyline view, bending the knee and looking up at the kneecap from below, I would have known right away in the operating room. The note I left in the folder that day is two lines. A solid feeling in the hand is not always the right answer, and there is no harm in taking one more confirming image. 02 “Should have just drilled the bone tunnel” It was a patient with a torn root of the medial meniscus. The meniscus root is like an anchor that ties the meniscus to the bone, and when it is torn the meniscus cannot do its job. There are several ways to fix a root. I wrestled for a long time in the narrow space at the back of the knee trying to stitch the torn site as it was, and in the end I finished with another fixation device. The operation was done, but it would have been simpler if I had chosen from the start the method of cleaning up the damaged root, drilling a small tunnel in the bone and pulling the root down to fix it. The folder name also has a note that reads, “Don't force a stitch at the back.” It means that it matters far more to decide a second plan before surgery, “if this doesn't work, we go with that,” than to change plans in the middle of the operation. 03 “Should have used a slightly smaller screw” This was a patient who came with a broken thighbone near a knee that had been replaced. It is an operation in which the knee replacement already occupies the space, so there is not much room to place screws. The inner surface of the lower thighbone slopes more obliquely than you would think. I knew it in my head, but when it came to choosing a screw my hand went toward “the longer and thicker, the stronger.” Looking at the post-operative images, I thought that if I had considered that slope once more, a shorter, thinner screw would have been enough. The same folder also has a note: “Holding the top of the bone with the instrument is harder than it seems.” There is always a difference of a few degrees between the textbook anatomy drawing and the real patient's bone, and those few degrees can only be learned in the operating room. 04 “I think I did it well, in my own opinion” It is not only confessions. The day I arthroscopically repaired a small tear of the shoulder tendon (rotator cuff), I carefully wrote on the folder name, “I think I did it well, in my own opinion.” I added the words “in my own opinion” because I know the real verdict comes months later, from the patient's shoulder. There are also many folders where I wrote down tricks I learned from other surgeons. In ankle surgery, where to open the skin so as not to cut the ligament twice When inserting a rod for a hip fracture, which way to push the entry point Some tricks were used in the very next operation, and some are still waiting for the day they will be used again. In closing: why I took out these notes Patients facing surgery often ask, “How many times have you done this operation?” It is a good question. I would like to suggest one more to add to it: “What do you look at again after an operation is over?” The number of operations tells you the amount of experience, and the habit of looking back tells you whether that experience turns into skill. My “should have” notes are an embarrassing record, but they are also the surest way to make the next patient's operation a little better. This evening too, I will probably create a folder and write a line after it. Hee Seung Nam

t: Surgery is a last resort, not the worst option
s: Common worries when surgery comes up, and what to check before you decide.
k: surgery fear worry last resort
b: Notes Surgery is a last resort, not the worst option Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · December 24, 2025 When I explain while looking at an X-ray in clinic, I often hear this: "I heard you shouldn't cut into a joint. They say if you have surgery you can't walk." It is natural to fear surgery. I too use it sparingly and say that we should first do enough non-surgical treatment, such as exercise, medication and injections. Why does talk about surgery sound louder? People who recover well quietly return to daily life. Experiences with disappointing results, on the other hand, are talked about for a long time and travel far. So cases heard from people around you easily feel as though they represent the whole. Distrust of doctors who recommend surgery also plays a part. Ask before you decide How far have non-surgical treatments been tried in my present condition, and can more be expected from them? What is the purpose of the surgery, and what could get better? What could happen if I do not have surgery? What are the risks of complications and the length of rehab? What are the other options? You may be told that surgery is not needed, or you may be told to wait and watch. What matters is not to decide in advance "I'll never have surgery, no matter what," but to decide together, based on evidence, with the doctor who knows your condition best. Getting another specialist's opinion when needed is also a good approach. This article is general information. Treatment can differ with the individual's condition and lifestyle, so please confirm through an examination.

t: The tip of my finger won't straighten: tendinous mallet finger and skin-tendon fixation
s: Diagnosis and treatment of tendinous mallet finger, where only the tendon is torn, and the technique and six-week recovery of skin-tenodesis, shown with real photographs.
k: finger mallet finger fingertip tendon
b: Hand The tip of my finger won't straighten: tendinous mallet finger and skin-tendon fixation Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · October 15, 2026 One person came in after pulling hard on a towel and hearing a 'snap' at the tip of the little finger; the end joint then dropped downward and would not straighten on its own. Because the tip of the finger bends like the head of a hammer, it is called mallet finger . Did a piece of bone come off, or is only the tendon torn? The tendon that straightens the end joint of the finger (the extensor tendon) attaches to the back of the bone of the end segment. If the end joint is suddenly bent forcefully, this tendon tears, or the piece of bone to which the tendon attaches comes off with it. Type Condition Usual treatment Tendinous mallet finger Only the tendon is torn, with no bone injury The basic treatment is to keep wearing a splint that holds the end joint straight for at least 6 weeks Bony mallet finger A bone fragment with the tendon attached comes off A splint if the fragment is small and the joint is not displaced; surgery if the fragment is large or the joint is displaced Before surgery. The end segment (the bone at the top) droops downward, but there is no detached bone fragment. During surgery. The tendon that straightens the end joint was completely torn. This patient had no detached bone fragment on X-ray, so I diagnosed a tendinous mallet finger in which only the tendon is torn. If left untreated, the end joint stiffens in the bent position, and over time it can lead to a swan-neck deformity in which the middle joint bends backward. Most heal with a splint For a fresh tendinous mallet finger, a splint that holds the end joint straight is the basic treatment. A review by a Korean hand surgery team describes continuing to wear the splint for at least 6 weeks so the end joint does not bend, then wearing it only at night for about 2 more weeks. If the end joint is bent even once during this period, the healing tendon can pull apart again, so it is important to support the finger and keep it straight even when taking the splint off. Surgery is considered, though, for people whose job or life makes it hard to wear a splint for long, who have skin problems, whose finger droops again after splint treatment, or in whom the tendon has healed stretched out over time. A Cochrane systematic review comparing splinting and surgery concluded that there is not yet enough evidence to judge in which cases surgery is truly needed. So the decision is made by looking at each patient's degree of injury and life circumstances together. This patient chose surgery in view of these points. What is skin-tenodermodesis? The tendon at the end of the finger is very thin and flat, so if the tendon is stitched only to itself, its holding power is weak and it tears again easily. Skin-tenodermodesis is an operation that removes a section of the stretched tendon together with the skin above it to shorten its length, and encourages the tendon and skin to attach firmly to each other. It is simple and gives stable results, so it is used when splint treatment has failed or for old mallet fingers. ① Stretched tendon Cutting across the end joint reveals the stretched, scarred tendon. ② Remove the excess tendon The stretched part is cut out in an oval and the end joint is fixed straight with a wire (gray). ③ Tendon suture The tendon is stitched together, and the ends of the suture are secured outside the skin and removed at week 4. ④ Skin suture The excess skin is trimmed and sutured, and the stitches are removed at week 2. The wire is removed at week 6. Figure. A simplified redrawing of the steps of the modified skin-tenodermodesis introduced by Professor Joon Goo Lee's research team. After the sutures were completed. The blue thread is a suture that supports the tendon; it is secured outside the skin and removed at week 4. The end joint was fixed in a straight position with a wire (K-wire). The 6-week recovery 2 weeks after surgery The skin had healed and the skin sutures were removed. 4 weeks after surgery The sutures supporting the tendon and skin together were removed. 6 weeks after surgery After confirming that the tendon had healed enough, I removed the wire that held the joint. For about 2 more weeks afterward he wears a splint at night that keeps the end joint straight, and from week 8 he moves it without restriction. On the left is 6 weeks after surgery and on the right is before surgery. The end segment that had been drooping is now straight. The end segment of the little finger, which before surgery drooped and could not be straightened on its own, regained a straight shape without flexion deformity and the ability to extend after 6 weeks. In closing If the end of a finger suddenly droops and will not straighten, suspect mallet finger and check with an X-ray for a bone fragment. A tendinous mallet finger with only a torn tendon is mostly treated with a splint that holds the end joint straight for at least 6 weeks . The most important thing during this period is not to bend the end joint. When a splint is hard to use, has failed or the injury is old, skin-tenodermodesis is a simple and stable option. Do not dismiss it as “just slightly bent”; the earlier you are seen after the injury, the more likely a splint alone will be enough. This article is general medical information. The treatment method can differ with the timing and degree of injury, your job and your lifestyle, so please confirm through an examination. References Lee JK, Kang S, Park JW. Cochrane Database Syst Rev . 2004;(3):CD004574.

t: Treatment options for tibial shaft fractures
s: Seven cases of tibial shaft fractures from stairs, scooters and car crashes, used to explain how to choose between intramedullary nails, plates and other treatments.
k: shin tibia tibial shaft fracture intramedullary nail
b: Fracture & Bone Treatment options for tibial shaft fractures Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · April 20, 2026 · Treatment choices seen through seven cases A tibial shaft fracture is a fracture caused by high-energy injury, mostly from stairs, scooters or traffic accidents. If it is not treated properly, malunion can change the alignment and have a bad effect on the patient's life. For that reason, a tibial shaft fracture has to be treated properly at the right time. Let me go through seven patients I treated recently, case by case. Case 1. A teenage girl who was hurt on stairs She came in after her body weight pressed on the shinbone going down stairs and caused a fracture. Not only the tibia but the fibula was also fractured. In the image you can see a displaced fracture of the left tibia. Because she was an adolescent who had almost finished growing, I used an intramedullary nail, which can treat the fracture without directly touching the fracture site. At 6 weeks after surgery I confirmed that alignment had been restored, and at 3 months the fracture line was almost invisible. In patients like this, a nail is a good choice. X-ray before surgery X-ray after surgery Case 2. A teenage boy who fell off a scooter He fell while riding a scooter and broke both the tibial shaft and the fibula. I judged that without surgery the alignment would change and the outlook would be poor, so I operated. On the AP image the difference in alignment may not look large, but on the lateral view you can tell that correcting the alignment helped. The fibula can be expected to act as a strut, so I did not fix it separately. At 5 months after surgery union was well advanced, and at 8 months I confirmed union. The nail is planned to be removed at 1 year. X-ray before surgery X-ray after surgery Case 3. A tall adult man in a motorcycle accident A young man who had a tibial shaft fracture in a motorcycle accident. What was unusual was that this patient was over 190 cm tall, so his tibial shaft was longer than other patients'. When I measured the length to the fracture site it was 390 mm. By AO standards the maximum length of tibial nail available is 330 mm, or 345 mm with the end cap. A nail is a good choice, but there is a limit to the instruments, so I performed plate fixation. After reducing it as well as possible, I fixed it with screws above and below the fracture. A nail of more than 400 mm would have been a better choice, but this is a case treated with a plate because of the limits of the instruments. X-ray before surgery X-ray after surgery Case 4. A tibial fracture in a patient with after-effects of polio There can be controversy in treating a patient who has had polio. This patient was active and loved exercise, so I went ahead with surgery. Because of polio, the patellar tendon of the leg was poorly developed and the space below the patellar tendon (infrapatellar space) was small, so finding the entry point for the nail was very difficult. After surgery the fracture line is slightly visible but the alignment was well restored overall, and since the operation the patient exercises freely as he likes. X-ray before surgery X-ray after surgery Case 5. A refracture at the site of an old fracture A woman in her 50s. In her youth she was treated with an Ilizarov frame at another hospital for a tibial shaft fracture, and this was a case in which a fracture occurred again at the site that had healed in a hypertrophic union. This patient is very difficult to treat. An intramedullary nail has difficulty passing because the inner diameter at the narrowest part (the isthmus) is too small, and if done wrongly there is a risk that the bone will split. For a plate, no product matches the contour of the bone, so it would have to be bent by hand in the operating room, which is also not easy. So I referred this patient back to the hospital where the Ilizarov treatment had been done so that she could be treated there. X-ray at the time of the visit Case 6. A young woman who fell while skating It was a typical unstable fracture with a large triangular fragment detached from the middle-to-lower tibial shaft, and a fibular shaft fracture was also present. Such fractures often result from a high-energy force, so not only the reduction but also the degree of soft tissue injury and the possibility of compartment syndrome must be carefully assessed. I treated it with a tibial intramedullary nail, but could not insert it as it was. I made a small incision over the displaced part, reduced it and then used the nail. When I inserted the nail during surgery a varus deformity appeared, so I removed the nail, corrected the alignment, checked the alignment again and then inserted the nail to achieve the final alignment. At 6 weeks after surgery the fracture line was almost invisible. X-ray before surgery X-ray after surgery Case 7. A 40-year-old man whose leg was injured by rebar The most notable feature of this patient was that the tibial shaft was impacted into the fibular shaft. This finding was also clearly visible on MRI, and attempts at reduction in the emergency room did not work well because the tibia and fibula were impacted. I planned the surgery in two stages. First I reduced it and operated on the fibula, and the reduction went well so the alignment of the leg was nearly corrected. Ten days later I performed the second operation on the tibia. When the initial tibia and fibula fracture is severe, I stage the surgery in this order to prevent compartment syndrome of the leg and to put reduction first. X-ray before surgery X-ray after surgery Summary We looked at seven cases. Even fractures that look like the same site must be treated in completely different ways depending on the patient's age, the cause of injury (stairs, scooter, skating, traffic accident), anatomical characteristics (tall stature, polio and so on) and past surgery. The most common and best treatment in the textbook is not the right answer for every patient. The case in which a plate was chosen because the patient was so tall that existing nails were too short, and the case in which, because past surgery had deformed the bone, another safest alternative was sought for the patient instead of a risky operation, show this. A doctor's role in fracture treatment does not end with joining the broken bone. The heart of it is to design the most appropriate method by weighing each patient's situation and the limits of the instruments, and to restore correct alignment and help the patient return to daily life and the sports he or she loves. Tibial shaft fractures mostly result from high-energy injuries. Please take care when riding a scooter or motorcycle, or when doing an unfamiliar sport (for example, skating). If you are in an accident, please see a specialist without delay and receive treatment suited to you at the right time. If you have questions, please write to doctornhs@naver.com . This article is general information. Treatment can differ with the location and pattern of the fracture, your age and lifestyle, so please confirm through an examination. t: Bone pain every time you sit: weaver's bottom and ischial bursitis
s: Common in people who sit at work for long hours and nicknamed 'weaver's bottom', ischial bursitis: causes, symptoms, a real patient's MRI, how to tell it from a lumbar disc problem, and treatment from cushions to injections.
k: buttock sitting pain ischial bursitis weaver bottom
b: Hip & Pelvis Bone pain every time you sit: weaver's bottom and ischial bursitis Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · September 10, 2026 Just as the lump on the outer side of the little toe in tailors who worked sitting cross-legged is called “tailor's bunion,” there is a condition in the buttock too that got its name from an occupation. It is weaver's bottom . The exact diagnosis of this condition, common among weavers who sat all day weaving cloth on a hard wooden chair, is ischial bursitis . A weaver weaving cloth on a hard wooden chair. An illustration made with AI to aid understanding. The bone that touches the seat when sitting: the ischial tuberosity The prominent part at the bottom of the pelvic bone that touches the seat when you sit on a chair is called the ischial tuberosity . It is what people commonly call the “sitting bone.” Between this bone and the buttock muscle (gluteus maximus) is a small fluid-filled sac that reduces friction, the bursa . What is interesting is that this area looks different when standing and when sitting. When standing, the thick gluteus maximus covers the ischial tuberosity, but when you bend the hip and sit, the gluteus maximus slides upward and the ischial tuberosity meets the chair with only fat and the bursa in between. Contrary to what you might think, we sit on bone, not on buttock muscle. Standing The gluteus maximus covers the ischial tuberosity and acts as a cushion. Sitting The gluteus maximus slides upward, and body weight falls directly on the ischial tuberosity and bursa. Figure. A simplified drawing of the structures around the ischial tuberosity. If you sit on a hard surface for a long time, the bursa is pressed repeatedly and minor damage accumulates. Then fluid fills the bursa, the wall thickens and chronic inflammation develops. This is ischial bursitis. Korean radiology research also names prolonged sitting and occupations with repeated irritation of the bursa, like weaving, as causes. A real patient's MRI This is the MRI of a patient who came with pain in the left buttock, in the area of the sitting bone. The images show slices in turn, moving from the top of the pelvis downward. Axial MRI (T2 fat-suppressed images) moving from the top of the pelvis downward. At the level of the ischial tuberosity, a white, swollen bursa appears on the right of the screen, that is, the patient's left. There is no such lesion on the right (left of the screen). Unlike the right buttock, a well-defined, brightly glowing (high signal intensity) mass of fluid is seen around the left ischial tuberosity. It is an ischial bursa thickened by constant friction and filled with inflammatory fluid. Patients like this complain, from the moment they sit down on the chair in clinic, of pain and stiffness as if a hard lump were under the buttock. In a Korean study that analyzed the MRI of 17 cases of ischial bursitis, the bursa appeared bright on T2 images in all, and its size averaged about 4.7 × 3.8 cm. In many cases there was bleeding into the bursa, or the wall was irregularly thickened and septated. So it is sometimes mistaken for a tumor, but it can be diagnosed on MRI from its characteristic location and fluid-sac shape. Who is the modern-day weaver? Weavers at a loom are hard to find today, but this condition is still common. People who sit to work for long hours : office workers who sit in the same position in front of a monitor all day, and people who drive for long periods Cyclists : those who put their weight on a narrow, hard saddle People with reduced buttock muscle and padding : when the buttock muscle has wasted with age or too little exercise, or the cushion covering the bone has thinned after major weight loss. In the MRI study above, too, the patients were aged 50 to 82 (average 64). People with inflammatory disease : with an inflammatory condition such as rheumatoid arthritis, it tends not to heal and to last long. Why it is easily mistaken for a lumbar disc problem Close to the ischial bursa pass the sciatic nerve running down the leg and the nerve that supplies sensation to the skin at the back of the thigh. So when pain radiates down the back of the thigh it can feel similar to sciatica from a lumbar disc. Many people dismiss it as simple muscle pain and suffer for a long time. Condition Feature Ischial bursitis It hurts right below the sitting bone and is tender to the touch. It is worse when sitting on a hard chair and better when standing up. Lumbar disc herniation or spinal stenosis Back pain together with numbness spreading from the buttock down the leg, sometimes with reduced sensation or muscle weakness. Hamstring tendinopathy or partial tear A problem of the hamstring tendon attached to the ischial tuberosity. It hurts when sitting too, but more when running or reaching the legs out while bending forward, and it can occur together with bursitis. Soft tissue tumor If bleeding or septa develop inside the bursa it can look like a lump, so it is distinguished with MRI. On examination I press on the sitting bone to see whether the usual pain is reproduced, and if needed use ultrasound or MRI to see whether the bursa is filled with fluid. In a Korean study analyzing 64 patients with ischial bursitis, 92% had pain on pressing the ischial tuberosity. Treatment starts with reducing pressure The most important prevention and first treatment is to reduce the pressure on the ischial tuberosity. Most people get better with step 1 below. Step 1 · Reduce pressure and medication Use a soft cushion, or one hollowed out at the sitting bone area to spread the pressure. A donut cushion with a hole only in the middle was originally made for tailbone pain, so if the sitting bone rests directly on the ring when you sit, it is not suitable. If you have to sit for long, get up and change position every 30 to 60 minutes, and add anti-inflammatory painkillers or shock wave therapy. In the long run, strengthen the buttock muscles to build the “built-in cushion” that protects the bone. Step 2 · Injection If it does not improve, a steroid and local anesthetic are injected into the bursa, or the accumulated fluid is drained. Because a nerve runs close by, it is safer to inject at the exact spot under ultrasound. Step 3 · Surgery In the rare case that it keeps recurring despite treatment, surgery to remove the bursa is done. In the Korean study above, followed for more than a year, 79.7% improved with step 1 conservative treatment, 17.2% needed an injection, and 3.1% (2 patients) went on to surgery. Patients with inflammatory disease tended not to respond well to conservative treatment. In closing If there is pain, and tenderness to pressure, right below the buttock bone that touches the seat when you sit (the ischial tuberosity), suspect ischial bursitis . When you sit, the buttock muscle slides upward and the bone and bursa take the weight , so the habit of sitting on a hard chair for a long time is the biggest cause. It can resemble a lumbar disc problem or a hamstring tendon problem, so if needed confirm with ultrasound or MRI. Most people improve with cushions, changing posture and medication , and injection or surgery is not often needed. If a sharp pain under the buttock comes every time you sit on a hard chair, it may be the body's “weaver's warning.” This article is general medical information. The causes of buttock pain are varied, so please confirm an exact diagnosis through an examination. References Cho KH, Lee SM, Lee YH, Suh KJ, Kim SM, Shin MJ, Jang HW. Radiopaedia.org .

t: Rehab after ACL reconstruction and meniscus repair
s: A week-by-week rehabilitation guide for people after ACL reconstruction or meniscus repair: brace angles, weight bearing, crutch schedule, exercises by stage, and symptoms that need a call to the hospital right away.

b: Patient education › Rehab after surgery Rehab after ACL reconstruction and meniscus repair Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 1, 2026 This is the rehab schedule for people who have had anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction or meniscus repair. In both operations it takes time for the new ligament or the sutured meniscus to heal firmly, so the brace angle and the amount of weight on the leg are increased a little each week. Exercise often, as much as you can! Week-by-week at a glance If the table is wider than the screen, swipe sideways to see it. Feature Week 1 Days 0–7 Week 2 Days 7–14 Week 3 Days 14–21 Week 4 Days 21–28 Week 5 Days 28–35 Week 6 Days 35–42 Week 7 Days 42–49 Week 8 Days 49–56 Week 9 Days 56–63 Brace angle 0–30° 0–45° 0–60° 0–75° 0–90° 0–105° 0–120° 0–135° Brace removed Weight bearing Toe touch 25% of body weight 50% of body weight 75% of body weight Full weight bearing Crutches Two crutches One crutch No crutches How to read the table Brace angle This is the range in which the brace lets the knee bend. 0–30° means you can bend from fully straight up to 30 degrees, and it increases by 15 degrees each week. Toe touch The operated leg only lightly touches the floor with the toes to keep balance, and almost no weight is put on it. 25%, 50%, 75% of body weight The proportion of your body weight placed on the operated leg. It is easy to get the feel by placing the operated foot on a bathroom scale and pressing down. For example, if you weigh 60 kg, 25% is 15 kg. Crutches Use two crutches up to week 7 and one in week 8, and walk without crutches from week 9. Exercises by stage 1 Early stage 0–8 weeks after surgery Knee extension With a pillow under the ankle, place both hands on the knee and press down gently to straighten it. Leg raise Lying down, lift the operated leg straight, pull the toes toward you, and hold for 10 seconds. Bend and straighten Bend and straighten the knee within the brace angle, focusing on recovering the range of motion. Heel raise Seated on a chair, lift the heels. The goals of this stage are to straighten the knee fully and not to lose thigh muscle. 2 Middle stage 8–12 weeks after surgery Starting machine exercises Start a stationary bike, leg curl and squat machine with light weights. Single-leg stand On level ground, spread your arms and stand on the operated leg to hold your balance. Wall squat Squat with your back against the wall. Control the way down slowly, and come up quickly. This is the period for regaining strength and balance. If pain or swelling gets worse, lower the intensity. 3 Late stage After 12 weeks Strength machine exercises Do leg press, leg extension and leg curl at a weight you can manage, and increase the weight once every 2 weeks. Single-leg stand on a trampoline Build balance by standing on one leg on an unstable surface. Brisk walking Walk briskly on a treadmill. Jogging Possible from 6 months after surgery. The timing of return to sports is decided together through strength testing and an examination. Contact the hospital right away if: You have a fever of 38 °C or higher, or pus or discharge comes from the wound Your calf is swollen and painful to the touch, or you are short of breath with tightness in the chest Your knee suddenly swells a lot, or the angle you could move before suddenly cannot be reached Your leg feels numb or the sensation is dulled This schedule is the standard guidance I give to patients I have operated on. It can differ with the surgical method, the shape of the meniscus tear and any other injuries, so please give priority to the instructions of the doctor at the hospital where you had surgery.

t: After hip replacement: discharge and outpatient guide
s: A guide for patients going home after hip replacement: suture removal and showering, positions that prevent dislocation for 3 months, walking rehabilitation, when you can drive, and symptoms that need a call to the hospital right away, with illustrations.
k: hip replacement arthroplasty THA discharge dislocation after surgery
b: Patient education › Rehab after surgery · Hip After hip replacement: discharge and outpatient guide Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · November 2, 2026 This is guidance for people leaving the hospital after hip replacement. The key is to be careful about posture and steadily increase walking until the new joint settles firmly into the surrounding muscles and joint capsule, especially for 3 months after surgery . Before surgery. The cartilage of the hip joint on the right side of the image (the patient's left) is worn and the joint space is almost closed. After surgery. A cup on the pelvic side, and a metal stem and round head on the thighbone side, form the new joint. After discharge at a glance Discharge Come to the outpatient clinic regularly for X-rays and examinations. Take the medicine given at discharge until the next visit. Day 14 The stitches are removed. You can shower under running water from the next day . 1 month Activities that involve long immersion in water, like saunas and swimming pools, become possible. Once you can march in place without a walker, try walking without a walker together with a caregiver. 4–6 weeks If the right hip was operated on, you can begin to try driving slowly from this point. 3 months The period of dislocation precautions ends. Long drives are also recommended from this point. Medication and wound care You can take the medicine given at discharge until the date of your next outpatient visit . If side effects occur or are suspected, please call the main number of the hospital where you had surgery. Stitches are removed on day 14 after surgery, and you can shower under running water from the next day. Activities with long immersion in water, such as saunas, swimming pools and bathhouses, should be done, if possible, after 1 month following surgery. For 3 months after surgery: positions that prevent dislocation When the head of the artificial joint comes out of the cup, it is called a dislocation . Until 3 months after surgery, the tissues around the joint are still healing, so there is a risk it can come out in certain positions. The basic rule is to keep your legs as far apart as possible . Positions to avoid Squatting Sitting with legs crossed Sitting down on the floor in a W shape Do this instead Sit on a chair (with the hips higher than the knees) Put a pillow between your legs when turning over Spread your legs when lying down Change how you live at floor level. If you were used to living on the floor, it is best to change your habits to sit on a chair and sleep in a bed. Put a pillow between your legs when you roll over. So that your legs do not cross when you turn from lying on your back to your side, always change position with a pillow or similar object between your legs. Small tips for daily life Avoid chairs and sofas that are too low, and if the toilet is low, a raised toilet seat makes it easier. So as not to bend deeply at the waist when putting on socks or shoes, a long shoehorn or a sock aid is helpful. When getting into a car, sit on the seat first and then swing both legs in together. Depending on the surgical method, the positions to be especially careful about may differ a little, so if your doctor has given you separate instructions, follow those first. Walking is the best rehab The best rehab after surgery is to walk steadily and increase a little at a time . Put your weight on the healthy leg, and gradually increase the weight on the operated leg. Increase the amount of exercise little by little within what you can do. Increasing suddenly causes pain and swelling, so it is best not to overdo it. Keep increasing the amount you walk during the first month after surgery, and when you can march in place without a walker , try walking without a walker with the help of a caregiver. On stairs it is easier to step up with the healthy leg first and down with the operated leg first . Please avoid, as far as possible, sports that put heavy impact on the joint, such as hiking, marathons, basketball and soccer. Driving If the right hip was operated on, try driving slowly from 4–6 weeks after surgery, and it is best to drive for long periods only after 3 months , once you have recovered fully. If the left side was operated on, please discuss when to drive at your outpatient visit. Contact the hospital right away if: When the operated leg suddenly looks shorter or is turned outward or inward with severe pain and you cannot put weight on it (suspected dislocation) When you have a fever of 38 °C or higher, or the wound is red and swollen with discharge or pus Your calf is swollen and painful to the touch, or you are short of breath with tightness in the chest When the operated hip hurts after a fall This guidance is general information for people who have had hip replacement. It can differ with the surgical method and the patient's condition, so please give priority to the instructions of the doctor at the hospital where you had surgery.

b: Research Research and Publications Hee Seung Nam, MD, Orthopedic Surgeon · Updated November 2, 2026 I test the questions that arise in clinic through research and bring the results back into practice. The research is organized by field, done with the knee team at Seoul National University Bundang Hospital and the bone and soft tissue tumor team at the Korea Cancer Center Hospital. 23 articles Journal articles 6 articles First-author articles 5 articles Published in KSSTA (official journal of the European Society of Sports Traumatology, Knee Surgery and Arthroscopy) 4 articles Artificial intelligence studies Featured research Level of evidence 1 · Randomized controlled trial · First author If you explain “realistic expectations” before surgery, does satisfaction after joint replacement rise? 172 patients about to have joint replacement were randomly divided into two groups. One group received the usual education only; the other received additional education that explained the recovery course and realistic expectations in detail. One year after surgery, 83% were satisfied, compared with 65% in the group that received only the usual education. The difference was larger in people with a constitution especially sensitive to pain (central sensitization). I also did a follow-up randomized study (2025) tracking the same patients to two years. The difference in satisfaction at one year had disappeared at two years . The effect of less pain and stiffness appeared from 6 months, and the effect on pain lasted to one year. It means that explanation before surgery helps people get through the hardest first year of recovery. That is why I take time to explain before surgery. The first study was published in KSSTA (2023), the official journal of the European Society of Sports Traumatology, Knee Surgery and Arthroscopy (ESSKA), and the follow-up in the same journal (2025). See the 2023 paper → See the 2025 follow-up paper → Analysis of 863 patients · First author Do iron injections after joint replacement help? I compared 863 patients who had joint replacement, between those who received an intravenous iron injection afterward and those who did not. In the iron group, hemoglobin fell less and recovered better at 2 and 6 weeks after surgery, and among those who had both knees done in separate operations, the hospital stay was also shorter. However, there was no difference in transfusion rate, complications or final functional outcome . Only by knowing both the effect and the limits can I recommend it to the people who truly need it. Artificial intelligence · 3 first-author articles Reading the outcome in advance from a single image and preoperative information I built a deep learning model that predicts whole-leg alignment from an ordinary knee X-ray alone, and it showed accuracy similar to values measured directly on a full-leg film. I also developed a model that predicts satisfaction after joint replacement from preoperative information, and a model that picks out cases in bowed-leg correction that need a two-level osteotomy. I think of artificial intelligence not as a tool that replaces clinical care but as a tool that double-checks information easily missed in the same image. Bone and soft tissue tumors: 4 articles The rarer the tumor, the more important the record At the Korea Cancer Center Hospital I analyzed the treatment results of extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma and myxoid liposarcoma, and the survival and complications of patients with a malignant bone tumor whose entire femur was replaced with a prosthesis. For tenosynovial giant cell tumor of the knee, I summarized how effective arthroscopic excision is depending on the extent of spread.
